#8324. New Interior Department Plan Prioritizes Public Land Sell Offs and Data Center Construction

The Department of Interior's 2026-2030 Strategic Plan proposes selling federally managed public lands to states, localities, and tribes, ending LWCF land acquisitions, and redirecting remaining federal lands toward energy extraction and data center construction. For hunters and anglers, this represents a direct threat to access across BLM, USFWS, and NPS lands that total more than 500 million acres.

The Department of Interior has released a “strategic plan” that could guide the agency for the next four years, and it includes the proposed sale of federally managed public lands to states, local municipalities, and tribes. The plan to offload public lands—or “shrink the federal estate”, as the DOI’s 2026-2030 Strategic Plan puts it—comes roughly 500 days after Utah Sen. Mike Lee sparked a major national backlash with his failed plan to sell some 3.2 million acres of public lands throughout the western U.S. in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025.

“The Department will work to decrease the size of the federal estate by offering to states, localities and Tribes the opportunity to purchase federal lands,” reads a paragraph on page 16 of the 28-page plan. “Through these sales, the Department will be able to focus its resources on primary federal responsibilities and nationally significant federal lands.”

The Department of Interior manages more than 500 million acres of public lands via the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), The US Fish & Wildlife Service (USFWS), and the National Park Service (NPS). According to reporting in the Washington Sun, this marks the first time that the DOI has ever announced intentions to offload public lands in a strategic draft plan. And it breaks “with 50 years of precedent that largely limited land sales.”

In addition to public land sell offs, the DOI’s new strategic plan, announced by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum on November 11, would end the use of the popular Land and Water Conservation Fund (LWCF) to acquire new public lands. The Congress created LWCF in 1964 to reinvest offshore oil and gas revenues into public lands and outdoor recreation. The fund receives $900 million every year from oil and gas projects. It was fully refunded and reauthorized in 2020 with the passage of the Great American Outdoors Act.

The plan also announced that the DOI will further consolidate its workforce. This comes as the agency has already shed more than 20 percent of its workforce or more than 13,000 employees, largely through efforts pushed by the now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).

Another goal of the plan is to use public lands that do remain in the federal estate to supply materials and energy needed to construct data centers. “By developing reliable and up-to-date inventories of national resource assets, Interior will help ensure a stable domestic supply of energy, critical minerals, raw building materials and other important resources to build and power homes, data centers and long-term strength of the American economy,” the plan goes on to state. “In addition to advanced mapping, Super Intelligence and scientific data will enable the Department to expand and develop our inventory of potential resources. Together, these efforts will help the U.S. understand and actively manage its natural wealth, encourage innovation and support future development.”

The plan stops short of announcing any specific data centers sites proposed for public lands. However, there are already multiple efforts underway to permit data centers on BLM lands throughout the West. One such data center project near Boulder City, Nevada, which F&S reported on last August, was approved by the agency before a Federal Appeals Board overturned that decision.

A November 6 report from Pro Publica revealed that the Trump Administration’s US Geological Survey (USGS) has determined that some 91.3 million acres of public land managed by the Interior Department have the potential to host data centers. The states listed in the USGS report are Alaska, Arizona, California, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Utah, Washington, and Wyoming. The Pro Publica report also pinpoints Sec. Burgum’s personal investments in the AI industry at somewhere between $18.1 million and $64.4 million.

Public land is hunting and fishing access. When the federal estate shrinks, so does the ground beneath your boots. The DOI plan doesn’t just propose land sales. It signals a fundamental shift in how the federal government views the 500 million acres it holds in trust for all Americans. Ending LWCF acquisitions cuts off the primary pipeline for adding new public ground. Redirecting remaining lands toward mineral extraction and data center infrastructure reframes those acres as industrial assets, not hunting and fishing habitat. This is the kind of policy change that takes decades to reverse.

#8323. The Best Ice Climbing Gear of 2027: Boots, Tools, Crampons, and More

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

The author, Anthony Walsh, heads up 'Nightmare on Wolfstreet' (WI6 M7+) on B.C.'s famed Stanley Headwall. (Photo: Sebastian Pelletti)

Overview: The best ice climbing gear of 2027 includes Petzl Dart crampons, La Sportiva Olympus Mons Pro boots, Black Diamond Viper ice tool, the Blue Ice Choucas Pro harness, and the Mountain Equipment Xenith jacket, plus proven picks like the La Sportiva G-Summit boots. Our testers climbed up to WI5+ and M7 from the Canadian Rockies to the Patagonian Andes, in temperatures down to -30°F.

Ice climbing is a high-stakes sport. Do it right, and you’re in for a meditative cruise with just the right level of spice. Do it wrong, and you’ll be left spooked, shivering—or worse. The difference often boils down to your experience level. But right after that comes your ice climbing gear. When you’re 100 feet off the ground, pinned to a silvery ribbon of ice by nothing but four blades of steel, you need absolute trust in your equipment. But how can you tell which products to rely on? That’s our job.

This season, our team of testers tried out 15 pieces of ice climbing gear that are either new for 2026-’27 or came out partway through last winter. Some turned out to be overengineered, overpriced, or poorly built. Others proved thoughtfully designed and dependable in a range of winter conditions. Over thousands of vertical feet of testing everywhere from the Patagonian Andes to the Canadian Rockies, we sorted out the bad from the good. Below: nothing but the best ice climbing gear available this season.

Weight: 11.3 oz (men’s medium) / 9.9 oz (women’s medium)

Pros and Cons + Novel and effective baffle design + Two-way zipper with bottom hem snap + Low-profile, elasticated cuffs + Impressive warmth-to-weight ratio – No way to tighten hood – Gimmicky and impractical hexagonal stuff sack

Mountain Equipment’s all-new Xenith is the big experiment in winter insulation this year. After a research paper suggested hexagons might be the most thermally efficient shape, the brand built the jacket with hexagonal baffles. (These weirdly shaped baffles also seem to limit down migration.)

Our testers found it extremely warm for 11.3 ounces (with 4.3 ounces of 800-fill hydrophobic goose down)—making it the ideal midlayer on -30°F days and nearly unnoticeable clipped to a harness on warmer ones. The Xenith’s low weight comes from its spare design. It has two hand-warming pockets, elasticated cuffs, a two-way zipper, internal drop pockets, a hem-cinch cord, and a hood. Downside: The hood can’t be cinched at all. Without a helmet to fill it, you’ll feel like a kid wearing your parent’s oversized clothes.

Weight: 8.5 oz Sizes: men’s XXS-XXL (the women’s counterpart is the M10 Storm Bib)

Pros and Cons + Surprising stretch and durability + Superior range of motion – No women’s-specific version

The M10 Storm Hardshell offers hands-down the best range of motion we’ve ever experienced in an alpine climbing pant. Thanks to a roomy fit, gusseted crotch, and slightly stretchy fabric—a mix of ripstop nylon, proprietary waterproof laminate, and a slick jersey backer—we were able to step high and wide without feeling constricted—a refreshing departure from the Euro-style, slim-fit trousers that have taken over the market in recent years.

“While transitioning from a panel of limestone to a hanging ice dagger, I stemmed my legs as far as I could between the two mediums and felt zero resistance,” reported Climbing senior editor Anthony Walsh. Some testers reported doing a full split just to test out the mobility. No torn crotches yet.

The rest of the layout is smart but simple. The thigh pocket, big enough to fit a smartphone, and fly are both positioned to remain accessible even with a harness on. “The zipper is on a diagonal rather than vertically-oriented like most other pants, so you can relieve yourself without a harness’s tie-in points or belay loop getting in the way,” Walsh reports. Elasticized cuffs keep moisture out—something we appreciated when spring conditions left our ice pitches streaming with water.

We loved how waterproof the M10s were, too. “I tested the M10s on some of the wettest pitches of my entire season,” said Walsh. “My ‘waterproof’ gloves soon wetted out, and my face had a steady drip of water coming off my nose, but under the M10 pants, I stayed 100 percent dry.” Credit goes to a lightweight, breathable, proprietary membrane and a PFCs-free DWR (durable water repellent) that boasted best-in-test longevity. After eight straight days of fighting up scrappy mixed lines in the Canadian Rockies, both the waterproofing and the fabric remained intact.

Pros and Cons + Legitimately waterproof + Decently breathable + Cuff closure keeps out loose snow – Not very warm

These insulated rubber gloves were originally designed for fishers, but nowadays you’re equally likely to see them on ice climbers, especially on steep water ice in the Pacific Northwest. The Temres 282-02 is the only fully waterproof glove we’ve ever worn, and they climb decently well thanks to a supple, dexterous rubber, and a wool liner that doesn’t migrate much within.

The Temres is not exceedingly warm, but for temps hovering around freezing (or those with excellent circulation) these are a fantastic, cheap option. Otherwise, buy a larger size and add a thin liner glove for deep-winter leads. A note on sizing: Showa gloves run small, so size one up from your typical ice glove.

Pros and Cons + Warmest technical mountaineering boot made + Easy adjustment with BOA system + Surprisingly nimble and lightweight – Expensive – Unnecessarily tall gaiter

Knee-height mountain boots are no longer just for guided Himalayan climbers. La Sportiva’s new Olympus Mons Pro—a 4-pound-4-ounce pair of “8,000-meter boots”—is a game changer for ice and mixed climbers who need serious warmth without sacrificing performance.

Our tester wore them on Field of Dreams (WI5; 250ft), Mixed Master (WI4 M5; 1,000ft), and M7 cragging. “I have generally cold feet yet I was sweating standing around in -5°F in these boots,” he said. “Despite all the insulation, these are plenty nimble for WI5 and M5.” The Olympus Mons Pro might be a couple ounces heavier than La Sportiva’s G-Summit boot, but it is drastically warmer and just as comfortable. Unbelievably, it’s also 7 ounces lighter per pair than the brand’s flagship leather single boot, the Nepal EVO, thanks to Primaloft Gold Aerogel insulation.

The one gripe: an unnecessarily tall gaiter. “With such a long zipper to get in and out of the boot, I’m less likely to adjust the Velcro power strap when I need to,” said one tester. Thankfully the external BOA allows a climber to adjust some of the fit on the fly.

Weight: 1 lb 13 oz (per boot) Sizes: 37-48 (half sizes)

Pros and Cons + Easy to adjust with gloves on + Highly versatile + Ideal fit for small and low-volume feet – Not as durable as they should be for the price

The G-Summit climbing boot accomplishes a small but significant miracle: It’s a double boot that climbs like a single boot. The insulated foam liner—combined with the wrap-around inner shell and external gaiter—creates an envelope that’s warm enough for high-altitude mountaineering, and yet low-profile and precise enough for hard technical climbing up to WI6 and M7. The rubber rand was sticky enough to provide purchase in foot jams on B.C.’s Stanley Headwall, and the Vibram sole gave testers enough grip to cross boulder fields and icy scruff in Norway, Patagonia, and beyond.

“I loved the BOA system for quick tightening mid-pitch and for equally quick loosening when I arrived at the next belay and needed blood to rush into my feet,” said Climbing Senior Editor Anthony Walsh, who was able to operate the dial easily with gloves on. The system eliminated heel-lift, both on-route and off. “I’ve front-pointed 10,000 feet in these boots and walked many horizontal miles. I haven’t received one blister, and yet I can still climb WI6 and M7 in them,” Walsh said.

Our female testers raved about the fit, calling it a serious game-changer in a world dominated by men’s boots. “Not only does this accommodate lower-volume feet, but the BOA ratchets tight enough to keep my heel down,” said one woman. “That allows me to climb a lot harder, for a lot longer.”

The boot isn’t totally waterproof, but its TPU coating, weather-resistant zipper, and water-repellant finishes kept our feet dry after dozens of days on ice and snow. “Lots of approaches in the Rockies have semi-frozen rivers at the base,” said one tester. “I punched through multiple, and never felt humidity or wetness.”

But while the weather resistance easily survives hard use, some of the plastic parts may not. One tester noted a sticky zipper and a peeling toe cap. Another reported that the toe welt quickly shows signs of wear and had to order a replacement after just a few weeks of testing. The toe welts on her second pair have held up fine. Still, if you’re hoping for a boot that will last you for years, you might want to get some reassurances from La Sportiva’s warranty department first.

Pros and Cons + Top-tier durability + Technical aptitude + Out-of-the-box comfort – Not quite warm enough for extreme-altitude objectives

Scarpa’s fan-favorite Phantom Tech HD offers the same climbing precision as the old Phantom Tech, with more warmth, durability, and comfort at just a 2.5-ounce penalty. Body-mapped insulation—micropile, aerogel, and PrimaLoft Gold Eco—kept our feet frostbite-free at -22°F (with vapor barrier socks) near Field, British Columbia, but we wouldn’t quite trust it on Denali. “The rockered outsole has a trail-runner-like feel,” said one tester. “I’ve hiked and skied many miles in ice climbing boots over the years, and the Phantom Tech HD is without a doubt the most comfortable I’ve used.” After a full season, our pair shows no wear or delamination.

Pros and Cons + Packable + Superlight + Five gear loops – Uncomfortable to hang in – Ice clipper locations reduce usability of gear loops

For multi-pitch ice, where hanging belays are rare, our testers gravitate to a minimalist harness like the updated Blue Ice Choucas Pro. Its UHMWPE construction is surprisingly durable for 5.1 ounces, and it’s fully featured: gear loops, a haul loop, four ice clipper slots, and leg loops that open for skis or crampons.

Unfortunately, Blue Ice sewed the clipper slots over the gear loops, so loop real estate feels a bit scarce. Nevertheless, it easily held a full rack of screws on Murchison Falls (WI4+; 600ft), but our tester noticed the unpadded leg loops on the free-hanging 100-foot rappel.

Skip it for cragging or steep terrain; it thrives on big days in the alpine—where a harness’s weight and packability make a real difference.

Pros and Cons + IP56 water resistance + Low operating limit (-20°F) + Invaluable for anchors and belay-station communication – Expensive

An IP56 water-resistance rating and a -20°F lower operating limit make the Rocky Talkies as well suited to ice as to the mountains they’re named for. We found them invaluable for setting up anchors in Ouray Ice Park and for communicating between multi-pitch belay stations. The only knock is the price, though most testers found the durability worth it.

Pros and Cons + Long-lasting dry treatment + Easy handling – No middle mark

If you’re the kind of person who prefers the safety and flexibility of a half/twin rope setup, you’d be hard-pressed to do better than the DYAD 7.7. Our testers used these ropes on everything from Bridal Veil Falls to ice park laps over a full season in Ouray, Colorado, and not even the wettest pitches iced them up or wetted them out. Cons: There’s no middle mark, and the ropes are pricey.

Pros and Cons + Many accessories for specific customization + High-performance ice pick – Shaft shape and handle is not suited for sustained vertical or overhanging pitches

Gently curved ice tools have fallen out of favor for the flashier, radically shaped Black Diamond Hydra, but the updated Viper still has a home in our quiver. Its 2.5-millimeter pick is incredible in ice, but the tool’s standout feature is its customization: it comes with modular headweights, a long alpine spike for snow plunging, a micro spike, a full-size alpine hammer, a micro hammer, and an adze. One tester, an ACMG apprentice alpine guide, found the mellow shape natural for sniffing out thin hooks on slabby, traddy mixed up to M7, versus an aggressive tool like the C.A.M.P. X-Dream. The knuckle-bashing shape isn’t ideal for overhanging mixed or WI5, but it’s a great option for moderate and big-mountain routes.

Weight: 1 lb 9 oz (per pair, with monopoint setup) Sizes: 34-44; 38-49 with extension bar (sold separately)

+ Extremely light + Solid climbing performance + Surprisingly durable + Wide range of adjustability – Aluminum heel doesn’t penetrate dense ice well

With razor-sharp points and a modular design, the Petzl Dart has been our favorite technical crampon for years. Its new aluminum rear section and linking bar save 4 ounces per pair and eliminate the need to jerry-rig fit with Petzl’s Cord-Tec Kit.

Testers climbed up to WI5+ and M7 with zero flex or shifting. Like the all-steel Dart, it’s simple to switch between mono- and dual-point layouts, and interchangeable toe bails customize the Dart for any boot, welts or not. Testers used these ‘pons on everything from Bridalveil Falls (WI5+) in Telluride and hard mixed cragging to big Canadian Rockies north faces, including Mount Robson and Mount Temple.

The geometry of the front point is just downturned enough to hook securely into ice, but not so aggressive that you have to adjust your technique to get a solid stick. In fact, most testers found they hardly had to double-kick at all to get a quick, reliable bite.

“The secondary points are far enough back that they don’t get in your way when you just want to use your front point, but forward enough to engage when you want them to,” said one tester, who wore them on more than 100 pitches this winter. He also found them blessedly intuitive to walk in: “Even when hiking up and down the Ouray Ice Park trails or navigating a mixture of rocks and ice between backcountry pitches, the Darts kept me secure and balanced.”

Cons: Honestly, not many. One climber found the newly slimmed-down heel lever tough to operate with thick gloves on. Another found the metal buckle fussy—though Petzl’s sold-separately Elastic Strap ($26) fixes that issue with a surprisingly durable plastic buckle.

Pros and Cons + Triple-grip handle + Flexibility and reach in steep terrain – Too aggressive for pure ice – Handle isn’t as ergonomically contoured as other triple-grip models

One climbing coach and U.S. Ice Climbing Team member used the X-Dream Total Dry on hard mixed routes in Ouray and D14 king lines in the Italian Dolomites. The first widely available commercial tool with a triple-grip handle, it gives you tons of flexibility and reach in steep terrain. But it’s too aggressive for pure ice, and the handle isn’t as ergonomically contoured as on other triple-grip models. Thankfully, the X-Dream’s all-around handle is available separately.

Pros and Cons + Modular head weights + Ultra-sharp picks + Adjustable handle size – Geometry isn’t aggressive enough for seriously overhung terrain

An impeccably balanced swing, ultra-precise pick, and a high degree of modularity make the Black Diamond Hydra our tool of choice for moderate and vertical ice. Interchangeable screw-on head weights let us dial in balance for any terrain, and the razor-thin picks—2.5 millimeters at the tip versus a 3- to 3.5-millimeter industry average—place like a dream. “I certainly appreciated being able to adjust the handle size to accommodate the difference,” said one tester, who swapped between thin dry-tooling gloves and thick, three-finger mitts. The geometry isn’t aggressive enough for overhung mixed, though, like the crux ice-dagger transfer on Dark Nature (WI5+ M5/6).

Pros and Cons + Lightweight + Durable steel + Seamless rotation + Easy to place – Spring-loaded crank knobs are sometimes overeager

We occasionally steer clear of aluminum screws because we find they bind up in plasticky ice. But the featherweight, all-steel Blue Ice Aeros are easily the next best thing. The lightest steel screw on the market, the Aeros are easy to start, easy to clean, and rack neatly on a harness. The three-tooth design seems to bite more reliably than four-toothed models, and we found the Aeros never bound up, even in warm, snowy conditions in Colorado’s Ouray Ice Park.

Ease of racking was another fan-favorite perk. You can fit six screws on a single clipper as opposed to Black Diamond or Petzl’s four to five. Credit goes to the low-profile aluminum hangers, which Blue Ice managed to trim down without sacrificing the size of the crank knob or the length of the hanger.

“The hangers are long enough to provide plenty of torque to easily turn the screw, and they’re simple to manipulate with gloves,” said one Colorado-based tester after a season of backcountry ascents in the San Juans.

The Aeros also offer a larger barrel diameter than any other screw we’ve tried, which means you can thread them into old screw holes in a pinch and still get a tight, reliable placement. The larger diameter also came in handy while setting up rappels.

“V-threading was a breeze with the Aero, providing a wide window of ice to thread the rope and get it back out with my V-thread tool,” reported one tester.

The only thing we didn’t like was the spring-loaded crank knobs. While some testers loved that they snap back into the screw automatically, others found that the snapping sometimes occurred prematurely, pinching their fingers or gloves in the process.

Buy in this order: boots, layers, gloves, then a big belay parka. Crampons, ice tools, and screws are easy to rent or borrow while you’re learning. Boots and apparel aren’t, and they matter most to your comfort on the ice.

Start with boots, because fit is everything.

You can find used boots for $200 to $300, but buy new if that’s what it takes to get a perfect fit. Visit a local climbing shop, tell the sales associate about your objectives and experience level, and let them guide you.

Layer for the conditions, and keep your insulation adjustable.

Carry two to three pairs. Wet hands are cold hands, so the number-one tip for staying comfortable is keeping your mitts dry. You’ll need:

As with boots, buy your gloves new if that’s what it takes to get the fit right.

Yes, eventually. Make it the last piece of your kit. A two-way zipper and interior drop pockets are nice, but warmth matters most. Standing around belaying in the snow can be downright frigid, and the bigger and warmer your belay puffy, the happier you’ll be.

Rent or borrow these until you know what you like:

Yes, but upgrade as you get more into the sport.

Buy safety essentials new. That means ropes, harnesses, and helmets. It’s hard to tell if used gear has been compromised, and trustworthy safety gear is the cheapest insurance policy you’ll ever buy.

For most other items, shopping secondhand can help you figure out what you like before you shell out for a spendy new kit. Try MountainProject.com, GearTrade.com, and eBay, or Craigslist and Facebook Marketplace if you live in an outdoorsy town.

Gear reviews are highly subjective, but we do our best to combat that by taking a slightly more scientific approach to testing ice climbing gear. At the beginning of each season, we wade through sheaves of PR requests, consider the specs and promise of each one, and then carefully select the gear we deem fit to test. Then, we do our utmost to get each piece in the hands of as many testers as we can—and in as varied conditions as the team can manage.

This year, testers picked and kicked their way up everything from steep ice in Colorado’s San Juans to long mixed lines on Mount Robson. Samples traveled from Denali to the Italian Dolomites to the Patagonian Andes and back again. We belayed through blizzards, swung into bullet-hard ice, whooped over perfect sticks, and cursed through some of the wettest pitches of our lives. At the end of the year, we compared notes and selected only the best ice climbing gear to review. Those are the products you’ll see here.

Anthony Walsh is a senior editor at Climbing. Based in the Canadian Rockies, he does it all—from steep ice to long alpine routes to rowdy mixed climbs. All those pitches have helped him hone two unmatched talents: suffering honorably in Arctic conditions, and complaining about poorly constructed gear in the most eloquent way possible.

Corey Buhay is a freelance writer and editor based in Boulder, Colorado. She is a current member of the U.S. Ice Climbing Team and has redpointed up to WI5, M12-, and D14 around the Colorado Rockies and beyond. She is a coach and board member at The Ice Coop, Colorado’s only dedicated ice-climbing gym.

Emilie Grenier is a regular contributor to Climbing who actually prefers climbing ice to rock. As a result, Emilie is hunting for frozen smears come September each year, and you can’t drag her out of crampons until at least May.

#8322. Skiers, Your Eyes Need More Protection Than You Think. Here’s What Doctors Say.

Catie Evans had been skiing for days along the Continental Divide in Colorado when she woke up with swollen eyes.

After logging multiple 12-hour days back-to-back, all while wearing glacier glasses, the avid backcountry skier figured she was just tired. But as she skinned toward Dead Dog Couloir on 14,267-foot Torrey’s Peak, she remembers, “I started to feel like somebody had thrown sand in my eyes.”

Eventually, with her eyes watering, she had to ski down with one eye covered, squinting out of the other with her friends guiding her.

Later, Evans tried to troubleshoot. Had she damaged her glasses without realizing it? Did she miss news of a recall? Or, throughout the multi-day trip, had she taken them off more than she thought, slowly racking up UV exposure in the process?

She’s still not sure. But, she’s not the only skier to experience snow blindness, and her experience illustrates the importance of eye protection at high altitude. While we often discuss features like fit, contrast, and style when it comes to choosing goggles, sometimes we don’t spend as much time thinking about what they’re protecting us from. So, we called up a few eye doctors to ask all of your burning questions about eye safety on the slopes.

While you might associate sun damage with summer days, skiers are constantly enjoying a double-dose of UV radiation thanks to the strength of the sun above combined with the reflective snow below. And, that exposure increases by roughly 4 to 5 percent for every 1,000-foot increase in elevation thanks to the gradually-thinning atmosphere.

Never let temperature or overcast conditions fool you; those invisible rays are always shining down, and they’ll pierce right through the clouds into your unsuspecting eyeballs.

We Tested 29 Pairs of Goggles. These are the 10 Best for the 2026-’27 Ski Season.

“Whenever we’re outside, (UV) rays can damage the surface of the eye as well as the cornea and lens,”  explained Dr. Becky Leenheer, spokesperson for the American Academy of Ophthalmology spokesperson, an assistant professor at the University of New Mexico, and an ophthalmologist herself.

Children, she said, are especially vulnerable. “Over time, cumulative UV exposure raises the risk of cataracts and of growths on the eye’s surface.”

Dr. Thomas Litzinger, an avid skier and ophthalmologist at ReVision Lasik and Cataract Surgery in Ohio, noted that the scariest potential consequence of continued exposure is cancers of the eye or the skin around it.

These conditions develop gradually, Leenheer said, but you shouldn’t ignore short-term discomfort either. Issues like photokeratitis (snow blindness), which is basically a burn to the corneal surface, hurts like heck and can contribute to further problems, though you may not feel them developing in the moment. Going forward, they’re a sign to protect your eyes better next time.

Here’s the good news: Almost any pair of goggles on the market should protect you from these risks. To be sure, look for claims like “100% UV (or UVA and UVB) Protection” or “UV400.”

One caveat is that goggles are not regulated in the United States. While any reputable company should be safe, we make no promises about the $20 goggles you found on Amazon. Litzinger added that the European Union does regulate goggles, and the label CE (Conformité Européenne) denotes that a pair meets EU standards.

Beyond UV protection, he explained, choosing goggles comes down to preference, or safety in the sense that better visual quality and field-of-view may help you avoid other accidents.

He notes that one common misconception is conflating UV protection with Visible Light Transmission (VLT). This factor determines how much brightness your goggles let in, but has no bearing on UV protection.

“There is no correlation between darker lenses and higher UV blocking,” added Dr. Cameron Cutler, an optometrist at Summit Vision in Frisco, Colorado. “Tint color does not matter, buy what you like!”

Features such as different tints, anti-fog measures, and lens shapes may promise improvements when it comes to comfort and visual quality, but they also don’t impact sun exposure itself.

Litzinger added that some skiers mistake glare complications for snow blindness, but this is another misconception. Though glare can be painful, or even reduce one’s ability to see, the cause is excessive brightness and likely choosing the wrong VLT for the conditions, not UV exposure.

As unpleasant as glare is, you can rest assured you’re protected from a UV standpoint with quality goggles.

Some companies do try to mitigate this issue by offering tinted, high-contrast or polarized lenses for a more comfortable ride. But be aware the latter poses a trade-off many skiers opt against, Cutler noted, as it can hide dangerous icy patches as well as glare.

Overall, Litzinger said, “It’s pretty important as skiers and riders to match your lens to the conditions to really discern contrast and terrain.” Additionally, Leenheer said, skiers should make sure their goggles are impact-resistant and fit snugly to protect you from wind, snow, and excess sunlight.

But, choosing the wrong ones (provided they have UV protection) won’t lead to any long-term eye damage, and neither will opting for budget goggles. “On the UV front, cheap and expensive are on the same playing field,” Litzinger said, adding that expensive goggles may distinguish themselves in other ways including fit, durability, and optical quality.

While some glasses and contacts block UV rays too, Cutler noted that full-coverage goggles offer the most protection for your eyes, as well as the sensitive skin around them.

That said, you’re only protected if you’re wearing them.

Plenty of eye damage occurs when skiers stop for lunch or a beer, take off the Oakleys, and expose their eyes to all those UV rays they’ve been avoiding all day, Cutler noted. So, even once you’ve taken off your skis, be aware of your environment and ready to rock eye protection for as long as you’re outdoors.

#8320. Lone Wolf Custom Gear Crossover Climber Review: The Most Ingenious Climbing Tree Stand Ever Made

I have been testing climbing tree stands for some 30 years now, and in that time, I’ve set up and sat in just about every model made, or at least some version of every base model made. For a long time—probably more than a decade—if you asked me, “What is the best climbing tree stand on the market?” I would have immediately answered, the Lone Wolf Hand Climber.

Ironically, that climber was not the easiest to climb with, and you couldn’t say it was built for comfort, but it was absolutely brilliant in every other way. It weighed nothing, folded down flat as a pizza box, was dead quiet, and bit into the tree like was made of beaver teeth. For run-and-gun—and especially run-and-bow—hunting, there was nothing better.

Well, now there is. The old Hand Climber is no longer produced, and Lone Wolf is now Lone Wolf Custom Gear, or LWCG, but their D’Acquisto Series Crossover Climber is everything the original was, only better. Here’s a close look.

The first thing to understand about the Crossover Climber is that it is uniquely designed for the mobile hunter—for folks who plan to walk far and frequently, often on public land, to get on bucks that other hunters may never know about, and for those who prioritize portability over comfort in a climbing stand.

So, if you’re looking for a cozy climber to scale the same handful of trees on a single property not too far from the truck or ATV—and there’s nothing wrong with that—then don’t waste your money here. There are far-less-expensive climbers that will do that job just fine and, in some ways, better. But if what you want is a climber that you can throw on your back and take anywhere with minimum effort, that accommodates your day pack so you don’t have to stuff your pockets and lash gear, that goes up quick and easy, and whose every detail is purpose-built for your style of hunting—if, in short, you want the absolute state of the art in mobile deer hunting gear, then there is only one climbing stand for you, and you might want start saving your pennies.

The D’Acquisto Crossover Climber is made of machined aluminum with a hammered titanium finish, which makes the stand ultralight and surprisingly quiet, even if you accidentally do bump the metal parts together. Although it is nearly the same size as the old hand climber, it is a full 5 pounds lighter at just 11.5 pounds, and it packs even slimmer.

LWCG kept the original traction belt and cam system for tree attachment, which works great and allows quick adjustments of the seat portion as you climb. Speaking of which, the seat portion now has a recessed, half-moon shape combined with a sliding web seat and removable cushion, an update to the Hand Climber’s rigid seat, which sort of forced you out toward the end of the platform. This new seat system allows you to get closer to the tree, giving you more room to maneuver when standing. The seat portion also adds a micro sit-and-climb bar, which you can use, not use, or remove completely. This is where the “Crossover” name comes from, because whereas Lone Wolf used to sell both Hand Climber and a Sit-and-Climb models, this one offers both options in one unit.

The bottom platform replaces the original’s stabilizing bar with a folding stabilizer that has integrated climbing stirrups, and the whole thing folds down and disappears into the platform for transport. Both the top and bottom portions also have newly designed recessed hinges that fold down perfectly flat. The stabilizing straps that connect the top and bottom portions while climbing have also been updated with metal, instead of plastic, buckles. Finally, there is a new tightening T-bolt that fastens the top and bottom portions together for transport, locking them in place—a huge improvement on the original stand’s bungee cord.

Related: The Complete Guide to Hunting Deer from a Tree Stand

Tree stands aren’t like rifles or binoculars. I can’t report my group-size measurements or scores in a resolution test. What I can tell you is that I have used the stand for a good part of the 2026 bow season so far, and, if you couldn’t tell already, I’m impressed.

The real genius of the Crossover Climber is that everything folds or hinges or meshes or integrates ingeniously to create the most compact and packable (not to mention the lightest) climbing stand on the market. By a mile. As I said, the original Hand Climber packed up as thin as a pizza box. The Crossover packs up as thin as a laptop computer, and the new tightening T-bolt system snugs the two portions of the stand together, so there’s no clinking or clanging while you walk. The stand comes with very good padded shoulder straps, and it is designed so your daypack can attach to and ride along with the stand. The mini sit-and-climb bar even doubles as a support for your pack.

There are a few things I don’t love about this stand. The mesh seat is a bit of a pain. Yes, it slides out of the way to give you more room when standing, which is great, but I found myself having to fiddle with it to reposition for sitting. And I’ll repeat that it is not as roomy or comfortable as many other climbers. You can buy an extension for the bottom platform that adds a few inches, which helps, but this is a small stand. (Personally, I would love it if LWCG came out with a slightly larger version, as I would happily carry a few extra pounds for more room—and it would probably still be lighter than any other climber on the market besides this one.) All of that said, this not a knock on the Crossover, per se, as it is designed to be minimalist. It’s just a fact that you should be aware of before you drop more than a grand on a climbing stand.

Which brings me to the one other thing I don’t love: the price. Oof. Maybe I’m a bad judge, given that I still can’t wrap my head around so many hunters wearing $200 pants. But $1,200 is a price I never thought I’d see on a climbing stand. Of course, I never thought I’d see $8 a pound for beef chuck, either. Everything, it seems, costs three times what it used to. So, I’ll leave it to you to decide if it’s worth it. What I can tell you is no other climbing stand on the market gives half as much attention to detail—details that matter when you’re hunting—as this one. It is brilliantly engineered. And if you’re a mobile hunter who likes a climber, it will be your constant companion and one of your favorite pieces of gear for many deer season’s to come.

#8319. How Joe “Stringbean” McConaughy (Finally) Broke the John Muir Trail FKT

Joe McConaughy thought he would probably start a bit slower than François D’Haene when he went after the Frenchman’s record on the John Muir Trail (JMT) this September. He guessed he’d be maybe 20 or 30 minutes behind in the early miles.

But when McConaughy got to Kearsarge Pass around mile 40, he was an hour off of D’Haene, who ran the Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the 223-mile trail through California’s Sierra Nevada in 2017, just months after winning UTMB for the third time.

“That was definitely a bit of a crack in the armor,” McConaughy told Trail Runner. “But I told myself that maybe he went out at more of a race effort, while my pace was better for a multi-day FKT.”

McConaughy, known by his thru-hiking trail name, “Stringbean,” has more than a few multiday FKTs to his name. He’s set records on the Pacific Crest Trail, Appalachian Trail, Long Trail, and Arizona Trail. And he had two prior record attempts on the JMT, one of which earned him an unsupported FKT.

“I thought my experience could help me beat him,” McConaughy said.

As he chased the ghost of the JMT’s past, McConaughy drew from his many multi-day FKTs and races. All of the miles and mistakes, successes and failures, and lessons and growth along the way helped him ultimately establish a new FKT of 2 days, 16 hours, and 15 seconds, taking nearly three and a half hours off a time that had stood for nearly a decade.

In rock climbing, climbers talk about “flashing” a route. It’s when they successfully climb the whole thing on their first attempt—without any practice or “beta” to help. McConaughy’s JMT effort was pretty much the opposite of flashing. The 35-year-old Seattle-based endurance coach was incredibly familiar with every mile of the JMT. Prior to his record setting attempt this fall, he’d covered the trail four times—the first in 2014—including the two prior FKT attempts. He’d also spent five summers guiding backpacking trips in the Sierra.

So when McConaughy ended up in a blizzard on Muir Pass with snowflakes landing in his eyeballs, it didn’t really stress him out or slow him down. If anything, it helped him move faster as he wanted to get up and over to warmer ground.

“I’ve seen the worst that the Sierra can throw at you,” he said, citing thunderstorms, blizzards, and rugged terrain. “I didn’t have to do a bunch of mental gymnastics, worrying about things I hadn’t experienced before. Instead, I could devote all of my energy to things that actually were issues.”

Most of McConaughy’s issues during the record attempt were ones he expected to occur, was prepared for, and could handle. “The long climbs were long climbs and some of the descents take decades,” he said. But after numerous JMT attempts he knew “it could feel much harder.” A little over a day into his attempt he was two hours ahead of D’Haene’s splits.

The JMT is far from the only goal for which McConaughy’s persistence has paid off. He took seven swings at earning a Golden Ticket into the Western States 100 before clinching one at the Black Canyon 100K on his eighth try in 2025. He’s also raced the Cocodona 250 three times and has a trio of Barkley Marathons starts.

“I like to think I’m more fun than a project-er, but when I look back, that’s pretty much my entire running career,” he said. “I feel like it gives me purpose. I want to do routes that inspire me and motivate me and take what I’ve done wrong, or what I feel like I could improve on, and continue to experiment, tinker, and optimize.”

He’s not as intense as a rock climber going after a seemingly impossible objective like the Dawn Wall, he swears. Rather, it’s about finding the sweet spot where he’s pushing himself to grow but having fun doing it. He’s not training to be the best at any given race or record attempt; he’s training to be the best version of himself for years to come.

“I get a lot of joy from sticking with the process, training with a smile, putting in the work to make a difference, and looking for opportunities to rise like a phoenix and perform the best that I can,”  McConaughy said.

Caroline Himbert, who is coached by McConaughy and set her own unsupported FKT on the JMT this July, helped pace McConaughy on the JMT this fall. “He goes back to things he’s failed at and tries to continuously learn and grow; he loves the science and spreadsheets and takes things seriously,” Himbert said. “But at the same time, he doesn’t take things too seriously and he keeps things fluid and fun.”

As evidenced by the fact that it stood for nine years, the JMT record was stout. D’Haene is known for bringing a newfound level of professionalism to FKT attempts, with a full support staff, set of pacers, and film crew. But rather than seeing the competitive level of the record as a deterrent, McConaughy saw it as part of the draw.

“It’s the granddaddy of FKTs,” he said. “More people have attempted the JMT FKT than pretty much any other premier route that exists—and the fact that François [D’Haene] and Darcy [Piceu] were the [previous] record holders is an ode to the level of attention and competitiveness that it’s gotten.”

On his first attempt in 2022, McConaughy set an unsupported record of three days and one hour. But Jeff Garmire beat it by 13 minutes just 25 days later.

McConaughy knew he could do better, so he tried to reclaim the record in 2024. But he hallucinated in the final miles and wound up off-trail on a class-four scramble, much closer to life-and-limb-threatening risk than he’d anticipated. It was a wake-up call for McConaughy, who always considers what he’s asking of others when he chases a big goal. He’s now the father of a 6-month-old and knew he couldn’t end up in a similar situation—or worse—if he went back.

“That experience made me really rethink what the record meant to me and ask myself if I wanted to do it again,” he said, adding that it felt reckless to go for another unsupported record. But after much reflection, and many conversations with his wife Katie, he decided he had to go back.

“I knew I couldn’t exist as an athlete without trying to put my stamp on the JMT,” he said. “This was my third time [attempting the FKT] on this trail and I wanted to give it my all, and use my best tips and tricks from every other effort to get the record.”

McConaughy showed up with a 12-tab spreadsheet and 12 years of beta to guide his effort this fall. He thought some of the greatest opportunities for improvement lay in fueling, pacing, and recruiting an all-star crew to help him out. In his unsupported-style attempts, he’d had to carry all of his own food and gear with no supply restocks along the way.

At Cocodona in 2025, McConaughy hit a wall that no amount of carbs could fix. He thought he knew how he needed to fuel to compete for the win. He’d done sweat testing and was experimenting with high-carb fueling. But he ended up with GI distress and struggled to breathe. He still finished in a respectable fourth place, but it was far from the finish he wanted.

He started working with nutritionist Meredith Terranova, who suggested he was likely hypernatremic—too high of blood sodium concentration—during Cocodona. He wondered if trying to optimize his performance through a data-driven approach with high carb fueling and sweat tests meant he’d stopped listening to his body.

So on the JMT he turned to real food like trail mix, purees, and waffles, especially on the big climbs—of which there is no shortage with 38,000 feet of elevation gain to cover. He also used recovery drink mixes and fat- and protein-based fuels from his nutrition sponsor, Näak.

“I feel like sticking to more whole food was the biggest learning and the biggest difference maker in my performance,” he said.

He also made up ground through a smarter sleep strategy. In his 2022 attempt, in which he finished six hours behind D’Haene’s record time, McConaughy slept for six hours. He knew there was an opportunity to trim down time spent resting while still sleeping enough to avoid dangerous hallucinations.

He settled on taking a mere 40 minutes of sleep beneath a pine tree on Bear Ridge—around 28 hours in. He thought it might be prudent to get at least an hour but he decided to push it a little with 40 minutes, figuring he could always nap later if he needed it. When he got to his third night out on the trail he was still running strong, cracking jokes, and appreciating his surroundings, Himbert said.

“You could tell he was having a good time and he was a ball of energy,” she said. “I was with him more towards the end, and he was still moving so well. I think that’s the key with this trail; it’s so challenging but if you can still move well towards the end then you can crack these times. I think Joe really nailed it, and it went close to perfect.”

McConaughy’s crew was one of his greatest assets. He learned some things about crewing the JMT after his crew missed him at Kearsarge Pass during his Pacific Crest Trail FKT in 2014. The PCT overlaps with the JMT for about 170 miles. He had to keep going on the PCT for two days with no sleeping bag, only a half-day’s worth of calories, and nothing warmer than a thin windbreaker. “We didn’t really know what we were doing,” he said. Hence the 12-tab spreadsheet this go-around, which was largely for the benefit of his crew and the complicated logistics of supporting a record-attempt on the JMT.

Part of the beauty of the JMT is that it offers an uninterrupted tour of backcountry wilderness. The trail only crosses the road twice over the course of the entire 223 miles. That’s also what makes it a bear to support. Meeting McConaughy on the trail required hiking several miles and thousands of feet of climbing to deliver food and gear. Pacers ran monster sections—usually around 40 miles at a time. But his crew of pacers was up for the challenge, with a collective résumé that boasted JMT FKTs, podium finishes, and 200-mile runs.

“Tara Dower talked about being a vessel on the Appalachian Trail, and I certainly had a similar experience on the JMT,” McConaughy said. “I was able to appreciate the beauty of where I was and the excitement of doing this absurd endurance thing because my crew was always filling my cup instead of making me pour things out to keep going.”

One thing that McConaughy has learned time and time again, is that he runs best when his cup is full.

“Gratitude and joy are the greatest performance-enhancing drugs,” he said.

While he was running, he thought about Katie, who was home solo-parenting so he could acclimatize to the altitude and run for 64 straight hours. He thought about his parents, who enabled him to get outside and run cross-country from a young age. He thought about the people who have supported his running career, and the friends who traveled to the Sierra to help him through the 223-mile journey. And he thought about the Sierra themselves, the mountains that have kept him coming back time and time again for the last 12 years.

“I run my worst when I’m thinking about how far behind someone’s splits I am,” he said. “When I caught myself doing that on the JMT, I thought, ‘This is doing more harm than good. You need to move forward at your own pace, and focus on the things that really matter.’”

After shaving over three hours off such a long-standing record, McConaughy hopes that he’s reached an end with his JMT FKT attempts. With all of the time and effort he has dedicated to the JMT, it feels a bit like a fairytale ending: “The princess was saved,” he said.

Now, he’s ready for a new goal, one he’s ready to chase to fuel his performance and fill his cup

“It’s one of those moments where I realize I’m maybe more capable than I thought I was,” he said. “And that makes it exciting to go back to Cocodona, or Western States, or another FKT, or any number of things to see what I can do.”

#8318. 4 Speed Records and Free Solos That Went Down in the Last 2 Weeks

Becca Droz (left) and Kate Kelleghan (right) set a new female speed record on the classic 'Naked Edge' in Boulder's Eldorado Canyon on October 26. (Photo: Jon and Jess Glassberg / Courtesy COROS)

Maybe it’s the erratic weather pressures of El Niño, or perhaps there’s just a particularly competitive spirit in the air right now. In the past two weeks, several climbers have broken records, made improbable repeats, and soloed terrain that would make many of us squirm.

Last week, we looked into the culture of free solo speed climbing in Boulder, Colorado, speaking with several athletes about the risks and influences they carry in their high-stakes sport. On the heels of this deep dive, two of the athletes who spoke to us went on to break additional records of their own within the past few days. This includes a new FKT on Half Dome and a fresh women’s speed record on Eldorado’s most famous route.

More broadly, we’ve seen a few historic achievements in the past couple weeks by free soloists and speed athletes alike. Here are four record-breakers we’ve been watching lately, in chronological order.

Just a few weeks ago, Alex Honnold told Adrian Ballinger that he thought someone would likely repeat his free solo of El Capitan before anyone dared to repeat his insanely hard linkup of peaks and scrambles in Red Rock. Back in 2022, he dubbed that linkup the Honnold Ultimate Red Rock Traverse (aka the HURT).

Honnold will have to eat his words, because on October 19, Nevada climbing guide Nik Mirhashemi put down the world’s second HURT, with slight modifications. Friends have been calling his revised route the NURT: Nik’s Ultimate Red Rock Traverse.

For the NURT, the 36-year-old skipped four non-technical summits, including Goodman, Buffalo Wall, Sandstone North, and Limestone North. Instead he traversed from White Rock Peak to ascend the seven-pitch Frigid Air Buttress (5.9+; 800ft). He then continued to the top of Icebox Peak. “Basically, I had to choose between adding Frigid Air or sticking with the OG route, where those nontechnical peaks are,” Mirhashemi said. “I didn’t want to skip Frigid Air as it is quite classic.” He also called the section he swapped in one of the traverse’s “routefinding cruxes.”

Despite the variations, Mirhashemi doesn’t think there’s a significant difference in effort level. He said that though his traverse is slightly shorter, he added more technical terrain, making the difference essentially a wash. “Nice to add a little personal flair to these things I suppose,” Mirhashemi said.

“I wanted to try the HURT for similar reasons to Alex,” Mirhashemi told Climbing. “Super long days of soloing moderate terrain is one of my favorite things to do. I’ve been coming out to Red Rock for many years and just moved here a year ago. I’m always looking for new ways to challenge myself and it just made sense as a goal right in my backyard.”

Last spring, Mirhashemi made his first HURT attempt, then completed several “scoping missions”  to prepare for his fall go. “I was never sure if I could pull it off,” he said. “Stoked it’s not haunting me anymore!”

Kate Kelleghan has been busy breaking her own record again, shaving minutes and seconds off the female fastest known time on The Naked Edge (5.11b), a classic multi-pitch in Colorado’s Eldorado Canyon.

Kelleghan, along with her French partner Laura Pineau, already held the record for the route’s women’s speed record of 37 minutes and eight seconds, which was 32 seconds faster than Kelleghan’s previous go in 2021 with Becca Droz, a Boulder-based climbing guide.

In late October, Kelleghan began working the route again with Droz. And on October 26, the athletes set a new record of 36 minutes, 26 seconds, shaving 42 seconds off the previous record.

“Becca and I were the team that started the women’s record, so taking it back together feels full circle for our friendship and our community,” Kelleghan said. Droz added that being able to track splits, as well as time out the approach, actual climb, and descent with their COROS watches “was a game changer”; both women are COROS athletes.

The men’s record is held by John Ebers and Ben Wilbur at 24 minutes and 14 seconds.

Just a couple months after smashing the speed record on the First Flatiron in Boulder, 32-year-old American climber Michael Reese established a fastest known time on Yosemite’s Half Dome on October 28. In so doing, he broke an 11-year FKT set by the late Dean Potter. Reese climbed the 2,000-foot batholith from the Mist Trailhead to its summit in 1 hour, 12 minutes, and 58 seconds. He followed Potter’s original line up Grizzly Gully, then free soloed Snake Dike (5.7 R; 800ft). He broke Potter’s previous record set on May 3, 2015 by about six minutes.

A few days after his Half Dome lap, our reporter Holly Chen, who also reported on his Flatiron speed record, caught up with Reese.

“In 2021, one of Dean Potter’s good friends told me about this as a potential record to try. He became one of my main climbing partners,” Reese told Chen. Since then, Reese has made 16 attempts and several scouting missions before his record-breaking attempt in late October.

“Records are made to be broken. I’m not gonna be surprised if it’s broken one day,” Reese said.

In the second-hardest free solo by a woman, Aleksandra “Ola” Taistra climbed a seven-pitch, 720-foot route in Sardinia, Italy on October 29. The line in question is Margarites (7a+/5.12a) up the limestone cliffs of Monte Oddeu. Established in 1998 by Andrea Calvo and Lorenzo Nadali, the route has become one of Sardinia’s “most sought-after lines,” according to Taistra. It includes a bouldery 7a+/5.12a crux pitch high off the deck; two 7a/5.11d pitches; and four additional pitches graded 6c+/5.11c, 6b+/5.11a, 6a+/5.10c, and 5c/5.10a, in order of descending difficulty.

“Climbing Margarites for the first time I thought that climbing it without a rope was impossible for me,” Taistra shared with Climbing, “and that’s exactly how the plan was born—first get to know the route, and then properly assess my skills.” Taistra says that when she finished free soloing Margarites, she thought: “Oh, that’s it?”

Taistra already put down one of the hardest female free solos in history in May, when she climbed Alfredo Alfredo (5.11d/7a) ropeless. Now, the only known harder female free solo belongs to French legend Catherine Destivelle, who climbed an unnamed route in Mali without a rope that she said maxed out at 7b or 5.12a/b.

In May, 44-year-old Taistra told Climbing that free soloing gives her “so much peace” and feels less stressful than climbing with a rope. The 44-year-old climber rehearses her routes on toprope until she feels confident in the moves.

#8316. The World’s Most Cinematic Trail Running Is Hidden Above the Arctic Circle

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Trail Runner’s travel columnist Andy Cochrane has run all over the world, including five trips to the Lofoten Islands above the Arctic Circle in Norway. He shares his hard-earned recommendations on where to run, stay, and eat, what to pack for the unpredictable weather—and how to get there.

As a travel writer, I fly an embarrassing amount. Over three quarters of a million miles in the last decade, or roughly three laps around the Earth each year. That’s a lot of time in a pressurized tube sitting next to strangers, but perhaps a fair price to pay for the privilege of running trails all over the world, from Patagonia to Morocco to Greenland. Picking a favorite destination is difficult, but often actions speak louder than words. I’ve returned to one more than any other: the Lofoten Islands in Norway.

Hidden a hundred miles above the Arctic Circle, Lofoten is best known for its Viking heritage, red fishing  villages, and dramatic coastline—sandy beaches, turquoise waters, and walls of rock that rise 3,000 feet out of the Norwegian Sea. There are very few places in the world where mountains collide with the ocean in such a cinematic way, giving it the best of both worlds—and incredibly unpredictable weather.

On my first trip to the Lofoten Islands in 2017, a snow storm shut down trails in the alpine, so I explored the lowlands, dabbled in fishing and kayaking, and enjoyed a nightly sauna. Since then I’ve returned four times to explore different corners of the islands and am planning to go back again next year, because there is still so much to explore, especially if you love empty trails and technical running. Here’s why I think Lofoten could be the next great trail destination and how you can visit before it gets too crowded.

The Lofoten Islands are an archipelago in northern Norway that stretch from the mainland into the North Atlantic. At 68 degrees 54 minutes north latitude, they sit further north than most communities in Greenland and all but a dozen or so towns at the top of Alaska. The chain consists of five main islands and hundreds of smaller ones, connected by bridges and underwater tunnels. (Oh, the joys of Norwegian infrastructure!)

Combined, the islands cover a total of 474 square miles, roughly the size of the city of Los Angeles. However, they are home to just 25,000 full-time residents, most of whom live in Svolvær and Leknes. Suffice to say, the interior is remote and rugged; it’s common to find yourself on a trail without a single human in sight, despite the lack of trees and views in all directions.

Although there are offshore oil reserves nearby, drilling is prohibited in Lofoten (unlike much of Norway), which has allowed cod fishing and tourism to flourish. The landscape is a mix of granite spines and tussocked tundra, with a few birch and mountain ash stands sprinkled in. When storms roll in—which they do often—there is very little protection, which can be a humbling experience.

The trail network in Lofoten is a patchwork of everything from unmaintained user trails to heavily engineered routes like Reinebringen’s 1,978 stone steps. As a whole they skew towards the technical end of the spectrum; most are steep, rocky, and stout. It’s common to gain a thousand feet per mile or more.

The vast majority of trails start near sea level and ascend through bogs and brush, climbing into the alpine via scree fields and off-camber granite slabs. Expect your shoes to get muddy and shirt to be saturated in sweat as you climb to the summit. Some marshes have wooden planks and some ridgelines have cairns, but they aren’t guaranteed. It’s best to always bring a good map and a better attitude.

While there isn’t an official count of trails on the islands, a good estimate is around 150, including everything from short beach hikes to high ridge lines. For ambitious trail runners, the Lofoten Crossing is an unofficial 100-mile thru-route from Delp to Å, and uses a mix of local paths, beaches, and roads. It’s a great way to see the entire chain of islands, even if it skips some of the serene trails. A few of my other favorites are the steep climb up to Himmeltindan (2,700 feet in 2.1 miles), crossing the interior of Vestvågøya from Leknes to the eastern end, and almost any of the remote trails at the end of the archipelago near Å, many of which reside inside Lofotodeen National Park.

Lofoten sees over a million tourists each year, heavily focused on the summer months. The crowds get so bad in July and August that iconic trails like Ryten, Fløya, and Mannen are probably not worth visiting. In the spring and fall Lofoten becomes a lot more enjoyable, because it offers more solitude on the trails, open spots at restaurants, and generally friendlier locals. I have a slight preference for the fall, mostly because I reserve most of the spring for skiing, which also is pretty great in Lofoten.

It’s also worth considering the weather and daylight. For about a month from early December to early January, the sun doesn’t rise above the horizon. Days lengthen dramatically in the spring, from 6 hours in February to over 18 by the end of April. The Midnight sun rises in late May and sets in mid-July, offering 24 hours of daylight for a month and a half straight. Almost too much!

Weather is fickle all year but especially in the spring and fall, as temps float in the 40s and 50s Fahrenheit. Snow usually melts in May and the mountains undergo a rapid transition to green. In the fall the foliage turns to a golden and red mix, storms begin to batter the coast, and the Northern Lights illuminate the night sky as early as September. Thankfully saunas are common and help make cold weather running more enjoyable.

Getting to Lofoten takes more time than most destinations in Europe. The drive from Oslo is around 20 hours and the combination of train and ferry takes even longer. The fastest way to get to the islands is a flight to Bodø and then a puddle hop prop plane to Svolvær or Leknes. This saves time and helps avoid weather-dependent ferries, but is often more expensive.

I prefer to fly from Oslo to Narvik, which sits on the mainland adjacent to the islands, and rent a car. The drive takes between 2-4 hours, depending on where I’m staying, but is always worth it for the views. Plus, public transit is limited in Lofoten, so having a car allows me to get to quieter places. For example, the cinnamon rolls at Unstad are to die for—but the only way to get there is to drive (or go on a 80-mile round-trip bike ride).

Traditional fishing lodges, called rorbuer, are built on poles over the water. Many have been converted to cozy places to stay. My favorite is Hattvika Lodge in the town of Ballstad. The restaurant next door, Fangst, is one of the best in the area. For those wanting to stay further off the beaten path, Nusfjord would be a great option. For a wider selection of restaurants, consider a stay in Svolvær or Leknes. Regardless, it’s important to book early, because the best places fill up months in advance.

If someone told me the Offtrail Ultra was designed specifically for Lofoten, I wouldn’t blink an eye. The 5 mm lugs are perfect in mud and scree, the toe grip is great on granite slaps, the integrated gaiter keeps out debris, and the midsole is stable enough for the dynamic movements necessary in this terrain. Hard to imagine a better fit, honestly.

Designed for cold and wet weather, the Run Cold wool socks are designed with high-impact wear zones to help them last longer, but don’t feel overbuilt at all. Instead they are stretchy and comfortable, with a seamless toe to reduce chafing. They work well with tights and running pants, which I use in spring and fall running in cold climates like Lofoten.

Over the last few years I’ve trended towards running belts, but I make an exception for a place like Lofoten, where you want to bring a few extra things. The Triack has a snug fit with almost no bounce thanks to a bungee system that’s easy to adjust on the fly. Plus, with four easy-access pockets, I can carry spare layers, gloves, snacks, water, camera, and first aid easily.

The name is a bit of a misnomer, because it’s actually made of merino wool. The wool helps regulate temperature better than other materials, keeping you warmer at the start and cooler when you heat up, not to mention not smelling after days of use. I love the hood and neck gaiter for colder days, and how the hoodie works great under a raincoat, too.

#8315. New Climbing Gym in Massachusetts Plans to Give Away All Its Profits

Berkshire Boulders General Manager Austen McNulty (left) and founder Nick Friedman (right) inside the gym. (Photo: Courtesy Nick Friedman)

The United States has become known for corporate climbing gyms and nationwide chains fraught with labor issues that charge high dollar. A recent analysis by an adventure travel company, which leverages 2026 data as well as the Climbing Business Journal’s 2025 trends report, declared that “the United States is the industry’s laboratory” when it comes to mega-gyms backed by private equity. As climbing becomes more popular, and thus more profitable, one may question whether these gyms will inevitably become the norm.

But in Great Barrington, a small town of a little more than 7,000 residents in Western Massachusetts, entrepreneur Nick Friedman is moving in the opposite direction: starting a new, independent gym that gives away all its profits.

You can trace the 38-year-old’s vision for an altruistic gym back to his childhood, when his dad put his career on hold to demand that General Electric clean up the river that ran through town—and Friedman’s property. In the 1970s, General Electric dumped polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) into the Housatonic River, so Friedman’s dad fought to hold the company liable. GE settled, paying $250 million.

In the process, Friedman learned the importance of activism. The cause close to Friedman’s heart is climbing access, which is not exactly easy to come by in Great Barrington or the Berkshires—but not for a lack of rock. While he calls the climbing in Great Barrington world-class, he says that privately owned land and conservation organizations that don’t understand the value of climbing make access a problem.

“Great Barrington is this unique case study in incredible climbing that is barred from true public domain due to land access challenges,” said Friedman, who has been deeply involved in local access work. In 2023, Friedman, who also serves on the board of the Western Massachusetts Climbers’ Coalition (WMCC), purchased a 70-acre parcel in the Farley Ledges climbing area. This bought WMCC time to organize the permits and funding to purchase it from Friedman earlier this year. While Farley Ledges currently remains closed due to an access issue involving a private landowner, WMCC is raising funds to construct a new parking lot and trail to reopen climbing.

Making these land purchases and forging the agreements necessary to maintain and expand access in Western Massachusetts takes a lot of resources, Friedman explains. That’s where his new gym, Berkshire Boulders, which opens on November 6, comes in. He plans to donate 100% of his profits to community organizations, including WMCC and Access Fund.

“The WMCC is very excited about the opening of Berkshire Boulders and the potential it has to positively impact climbing access in Western Massachusetts,” said Regina Madden, a WMCC board member and chair of its communications committee. Protecting and maintaining access requires ongoing resources, so a local business committed to supporting that mission creates an excellent opportunity. In addition, Berkshire Boulders can serve to bridge the gap between indoor and outdoor climbing, helping to foster a stronger sense of stewardship and community.

While Friedman may pursue nonprofit status down the line, he says it was faster to get the gym off the ground as a business that gave away its profits, rather than a 501(c)3 nonprofit. And as someone who has specialized professionally in startups, he adds that he’s always been “intrigued” by hybrid models that blend for-profit business models with nonprofit values.

Currently, the organizations Berkshire Boulders plans to support include WMCC and Access Fund, as well as non-climbing local organizations including the Railroad Street Youth Project and Greenagers, which fosters sustainability work among youth.

“I felt that a climbing gym could play a central role in that effort and become this anchor and the starting point for a broader vision of bringing outdoor recreation more front and center in this small town,” Friedman said.

Friedman doesn’t see accessibility as a binary, “indoors or outdoors” issue; he views it holistically. This is why he’s made it the gym’s mission to improve climbing access indoors and out. He envisions a gym as a place where you can learn the sport, meet partners, and find people to help you make the gym-to-crag transition. In Friedman’s view, that gym-to-crag transition is the end game. That’s why he decorated Berkshire Boulders’ walls with photographs of Great Barrington rock, and rents out crashpads to climbers who want to try bouldering outside, but lack the gear.

But the other end game is community, which he says is hard to foster when you’re answering to private equity investors. Berkshire Boulders’ KPIs will instead revolve “around community impact.”

One way he’s doing that is by offering hardship memberships. Each month, Berkshire Boulders will award free memberships to low-income individuals through a lottery system. This addresses the known problem of affordability in the gym industry—one so notable that the American Alpine Club declared it an access issue in 2024. Friedman says he’s already approved one hardship membership application, but doesn’t have a monthly quota in mind yet. “We do expect to expand that program significantly over the next several months,” Friedman said.

A focus on community KPIs, however, will not come at the expense of a high-quality bouldering facility. Friedman insists that he is committed to a top-tier facility. He is partnering with local hold-maker Decoy and plans to change the setting across the 15-foot-high walls every two weeks. The gym also features a custom-built, “artistically created” adjustable spray wall. Using the Clift app, climbers will be able to set sequences, replicate local outdoor problems, and track leaderboards.

Currently, for Friedman, Berkshire Boulders is a passion project. His personal endgame is not to make a living off the gym—he still works full-time as the chief strategy officer at a small-batch cannabis startup. He also hired an experienced general manager to run the gym. Rather, that Friedman hopes to ultimately do is drive positive change in his local climbing community.

“Personally, I would love to see the Great Barrington climbing become a published resource for the public,” Friedman said. It’s a long game, but a worthy one, in his view, to turn the local climbing from an underground, tricky access dance to a veritable destination with routes documented on Mountain Project, a guidebook, and formal parking and approach trails.

Beyond local impact, could Berkshire Boulders, if successful, inspire a rising tide of small, mission-driven gyms in this era of indoor climbing corporatization? Friedman believes smaller gyms with a focus on community have a better shot at bringing together passionate climbers than the larger conglomerate gyms. “I would love to see an expansion of smaller independent gyms regionally,” he says.

#8314. Minnesota’s Voyageurs National Park Named 2026 Dark Sky Place of the Year

Voyageurs National Park Dark Sky. (Photo: Daniel Dendler)

For people living beneath the artificial glow of city lights, a sky filled with thousands of stars can seem like something out of science fiction. According to a recent National Park Service report, 80 percent of Americans cannot see the Milky Way from their homes.

But at Minnesota’s Voyageurs National Park, a roughly five-hour drive from Minneapolis, some of the darkest skies in the country reveal the heavens in dazzling detail. And thanks to the park’s growing lineup of in-person and virtual programs, you don’t have to travel to the North Woods to experience the magic.

This week, Voyageurs received one of the highest honors in conservation: DarkSky International’s 2026 Dark Sky Place of the Year award. The annual award honors individuals and organizations dedicated to protecting nighttime environments. Voyageurs is only the second American national park to receive the award; the first was Grand Canyon National Park in 2019.

“What makes this award so meaningful is that it isn’t about Voyageurs being a beautiful place to see the stars. We were certified as an International Dark Sky Park in 2020 for that,” Christina Hausman Rhode, executive director of Voyageurs Conservancy, its nonprofit partner of the park, told Outside.

Since earning its International Dark Sky Park certification in 2020, Voyageurs has introduced some 8,300 students to the wonders overhead through its Virtual Dark Sky Classroom, welcomed nearly 6,000 people to Park After Dark and other nighttime programs, and drawn more than 1,300 visitors to six annual Star Parties. Add to that roughly 40,000 students nationwide who participate in Boreal Stargazing Week each year, and it’s clear the park’s reach extends well beyond its 218,000-acre boundary.

This honor recognizes what has happened since, Rhode added: “A shared commitment by the National Park Service, Voyageurs Conservancy, and our gateway communities to protect these skies and share them with as many people as possible.“

Voyageurs also stands out because it’s about 40 percent water—covered by interconnected glacial lakes—a fact that adds to its stargazing prowess. Sweeping views are unobstructed by foothills, and its 30 calm lake surfaces act as mirrors reflecting the constellations and making the dark-sky experience all the more impressive. This is no Great Smoky Mountains National Park with its 12 million annual visitors either. With roughly 200,000 visitors each year, Voyageurs offers plenty of wide open space to take in the starscape.

“Voyageurs doesn’t just protect some of the darkest skies remaining in North America,” Ruskin Hartley, CEO and executive director of DarkSky International, told Outside via email. “It’s the people behind that protection.”

Hartley said that from the land managers and rangers to community partners, there’s a shared commitment at the park to preserve the night through responsible lighting, as well as to share the park’s wonders with the public.

The recognition comes at the end of a particularly challenging year for wilderness conservation in northern Minnesota. In April, Congress passed and President Donald Trump signed a resolution that reversed a 20-year mining ban covering roughly 350 square miles of Superior National Forest near the neighboring Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness. The move reopened the door to proposed copper and nickel mining operations.

The threat to Voyageurs? Well, what happens in the Boundary Waters doesn’t necessarily stay in the Boundary Waters. The two protected landscapes are linked by the Rainy River watershed, a sprawling network of lakes, rivers, and wetlands. (Incidentally, the Boundary Waters and Voyageurs, along with Ontario’s Quetico Provincial Park, form one of the world’s largest dark-sky regions.)

“Copper mining from a proposed Twin Metals mine would absolutely impact Voyageurs,” says Libby London, communications director for the nonprofit Save the Boundary Waters.

Once pollution reaches the water, it can spread quickly for several hundred miles, explains Pete Marshall, communications director for Friends of the Boundary Waters Wilderness, another nonprofit organization that’s been advocating for the Boundary Waters area for 50 years. Governor Tim Walz signed an executive order in August to block the state from permitting copper mines in the watershed, but that order expires three months after Walz leaves office.

In July, lightning-sparked wildfires fueled by hot and windy conditions forced the rare closure of Boundary’s entire million-acre wilderness, upending summer travel plans and prompting evacuations. Out of an abundance of caution, Voyageurs officials banned campfires and charcoal grills for six weeks.

Against that backdrop, Voyageurs’ Dark Sky Place of the Year award is a welcome conservation victory.

Protecting the night sky at Voyageurs has required more than simply keeping the lights off, of course. The park has had to rethink how it uses light in the first place. Under a new lighting management plan, outdoor fixtures were replaced with dark-sky-friendly alternatives that direct light downward rather than into the sky. National Park Service staff also began regularly visiting five locations throughout the park to measure the darkness using a sky quality meter, a device that measures the brightness of the night sky. On a scale where 22.0 represents the darkest natural night sky, Voyageurs averages an impressive 21.45—meaning that when the sun goes down, the stars really do come out.

And while the award puts Voyageurs in the spotlight, the park’s greatest achievement may be what happens when the lights stay out. For Rhode and the Voyageurs Conservancy, the hope is that the recognition inspires others to look up—and take action.
