#8312. B.C. Hikers Were Killed in a Rare Predatory Grizzly Attack, Wildlife Officials Say

A grizzly, photographed at Vancouver's Grouse Mountain in 2025. (Photo: Gabriel Mello / Moment via Getty)

Wildlife officials in British Columbia said on Tuesday that they had caught and euthanized the grizzlies involved in a fatal attack on two hikers near Bella Coola earlier this month.

In a press conference , B.C. Conservation Officer Service Inspector Jeff Tyre said that DNA testing had “conclusively linked” the female bear and her three cubs to the deaths of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and Selah Reed, 20, the mother and daughter who died in the incident

“[The bears] all had to be destroyed, because bears that are involved in fatal attacks on people cannot be rehabilitated or relocated,” Tyre said. “This type of behavior presents an extreme risk to the public, and such bears are dispatched to protect the public and prevent similar attacks in the future.”

Notably, Tyre said that forensic evidence from the scene of the attacks led authorities to believe that the bears’ attack on Balcarras and Reed had been predatory, rather than defensive. Such attacks are unusual: A 2019 analysis of brown bear attacks in North America, Europe, and Asia found that only about 5 percent were primarily predatory in nature. In contrast, 47 percent began after the victims encountered a female bear with cubs, 20 percent after a sudden encounter, and 17 percent began due to the presence of a dog.

Balcarras and Reed had gone on a hike near their home on October 31. When they had not returned home the next morning, family members reported them missing. Search personnel found Balcarras deceased on November 2, and Reed the following day, both of them with injuries consistent with a bear attack.

According to a GoFundMe page established to provide for Balcarras and Reed’s funeral expenses, Balcarras, an art therapist, had only recently moved to Bella Coola. An obituary for Balcarras called her “a gracious, warm-hearted woman” who “believed in accepting people without judgement and showing kindness to everyone who crossed her path. Reed, who worked as an educational assistant, shared her mother’s interest in art, and had recently finished three large murals at Bella Coola’s health center.

The tragedy occurred nearly a year after a bear severely injured three children and an adult chaperone who were on a school field trip at a spot just miles away. That bear was never captured, and some observers speculated that the same animal could have been responsible for the deaths. However, Tyre said that the bears that conservation officers had destroyed were not involved in the earlier incident.

In the wake of Balcarras’s and Reed’s deaths, the Nuxalk Nation, the Indigenous community in Bella Coola, began to recommend an 8 p.m. curfew to local residents. Samuel Schooner, the Nation’s elected chief councillor, said that the incident had been “deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year’s attack.”

“We still have community supports in place, and they will remain there until we feel the timing is right to remove them,” he said. “Our community is rightfully still deeply affected, and will be for generations.”

#8311. The Best Trail Running Shoes for Fall 2026

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

The best trail running shoes boost our confidence on singletrack to scree fields, sand to slick rock. They’re comfortable and nimble and help us run fast or forever, depending on the adventure. As the days grow shorter and colder we’re also looking for shoes that excel under a wide variety of circumstances, like wet leaves, rime ice, and snow. And as the weather deteriorates, we’re also leaning more on road-to-trail models for the days when the roads and paths are calling our names.

Over two to four months of testing on varied terrain across Santa Barbara to Boulder and Nebraska to New Hampshire, our testers Lisa Jhung, Cory Smith, Johnathan Beverly, and Abby Levene provided detailed feedback on fit, comfort, speed, traction, cushioning, and their joy of running. The result is Trail Runner Magazine’s best trail shoes for fall 2026. Considering that the “best” shoe can run differently on someone else’s feet, our review is specially curated with a shoe claiming the title of each chosen category it achieves best. For even more models, check out Outside’s guide to best trail running shoes for fall.

Weight: 7.5 ounces (men’s 8.5), 6.2 ounces (women’s 8) Stack Height: 28.5–21.5 mm Drop: 7 mm Sizing: 7-12.5, 13, 14, 15 (men’s), 6-11 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Responsive and springy + Weightless feeling underfoot + Good ground feel + Excellent traction – Runs small (go half a size up) –Expensive

If the Norda 005 was a car, it would be the Mercedes AMG E63S Wagon. That is to say: it’s quiet performance luxury. IYKYK, as the kids say. Coming in at just 214 grams (7.5 ounces) for a men’s U.S. 8.5, it’s one of the lightest trail running shoes on the market. It’s also made from the highest quality materials: A Biodyneema upper makes it both durable and highly breathable. A slick of Vibram “Megagrip Elite” rubber renders the outsole ultra tacky on the trails while rolling over the roads. And, perhaps most importantly, the midsole is made completely from a proprietary Mouse Arnitel TPEE—a supercritical foam generally only used in small amounts because of the cost—making the shoe featherlight, energetic, and highly durable.

And the simplicity of the design lets the quality shine. As such, it’s a light, fast trail running shoe that can do it all. We’d turn to this shoe for anything from easy days on mixed surfaces, to “fast” trail 100-milers like Western States or Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc. Trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene wore one pair of the Norda 005 for the Tour du Mont Blanc, a five-day, 110-mile adventure through the Alps, and she didn’t think about her feet once. There is no higher praise.

The midsole is tuned to be slightly firmer than the superfoam in road racers and thus provides an energetic, bouncy ride that doesn’t trampoline you in wild directions off the trail. While the lack of a plate may disqualify the Norda 005 from being a true trail “super shoe,” don’t mistake semantics for inferiority. We didn’t miss a carbon plate here, and its absence allows for enhanced ground feel and adaptability to varied terrain. The foam and rocker deliver a smooth roll and plenty of precision.

The only real downside to this shoe is the price tag. But sometimes, you get what you pay for. Read our full review of the Norda 005.

Weight: 9.5 oz (men’s), 8.4 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 32–28 mm Drop: 4 mm Sizing: 7-13, 14, 15 (men’s), 5-12 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Excellent traction + Lightweight and nimble – Slippery laces require double-knotting

We’ve tested every version of the Saucony Peregrine since the model’s debut in 2011, and this sixteenth iteration just might be our all-time favorite. The shoe has long been capable of making us feel nimble on rugged terrain, with its great balance of ground feel and cushioning, plus traction on all kinds of trail, wrapped up in a lightweight package. But version 16 takes the Peregrine’s trail capabilities to new levels, and at $150, it’s an easy pick for Best Value.

The upgraded Vibram Megagrip outsole grips rock slabs with aplomb, while the four-millimeter lugs dig into loose dirt and soft ground (though some sandy-trail testers craved even deeper, toothier lugs). The balanced midsole—not too springy, not too mushy, not too thick—delivers a strong connection to the trail while still feeling responsive and shock absorbing, even during wild descents. The flexible, breathable mesh upper with added toe protection kept out trail debris and warded off snags from roots and branches.

The fit of this trail running shoe somehow made a variety of testers feel like it was custom-made for them. It locks down the heel, and the just-roomy-enough toebox allowed toe space to breathe while maintaining control. “The fit is just perfect,” said a tester. “I feel secure and supported from heel to toe, and side to side.”

Weight: 10 oz (men’s), 9 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 33.5 mm–25.5 mm Drop: 8mm Sizing: 7-13, 14 (men’s), 5-11 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Great traction + Outstanding foothold – Cushioning may feel too firm for some

The Salomon Genesis 2 earned mountain-goat status among our crew, providing outstanding traction over loose dirt and rock. Its supportive Matryx upper—constructed with thin, high-tenacity yarns and durable Kevlar—secures narrow and wide feet alike via Salomon’s quick-pull lacing system. The forefoot offers slightly more room than version 1, enhancing overall comfort without sacrificing agility.

The outsole, made of Salomon’s Contagrip rubber with toothy, 4 mm lugs, provided excellent traction on all surfaces, giving us confidence, even on scrambles over large rocky slabs and slippery descents.

While the EVA-blend midsole runs firm, it offers direct trail feedback. “This shoe makes it fun to pick a line and charge,” noted one tester. “I felt completely present instead of mindlessly rolling over obstacles.”

For technical runners who prefer softer cushioning, we also recommend the La Sportiva Prodigio Pro. (Read our full review of the La Sportiva Prodigio Pro here.)

The Nike Trail Pegasus 5 has been our top choice for road-to-trail runs for several seasons, so we were concerned that its newly branded replacement, the Nike ACG Pegasus Trail, would mess with its winning formula. But as soon as we stepped into the new model, we breathed a sigh of relief. The shoe is just as comfortable as its predecessor and, after testing, has proven to be just as capable on and off roads and over gravel, continuing its reign as the most versatile shoe in this roundup.

The midsole foam—Nike’s injection-molded ReactX—feels responsive and cushions comfortably on concrete, pavement, and hard-packed dirt. The outsole traction, from 3.5 mm lugs made of the brand’s proprietary “All Terrain Compound 2.0,” is tackier on wet terrain than the previous version, but still pales in comparison to Vibram MegaGrip.

What makes this shoe work from roads to singletrack trails is the fit and foothold. Even our most narrow-footed testers felt a secure hold without any pressure points, which allows precise footing on trails, no matter how steep or rocky. Pros and Cons + Extremely lightweight for a 40 mm stack + Great stability – Premium pricetag

Brooks has a reputation for building a great shoe and sticking to that formula, giving loyal fans a consistent ride, model after model. The tradeoff? It can make the brand seem boring. The all-new Brooks Cascadia Elite shatters that mold. It’s one of the most exciting shoes Brooks has launched in years, and arguably one of the most exciting trail releases of the year.

Despite sharing a name, the Cascadia Elite is nothing like the everyday, cushioned Cascadia trail runner: It’s a trail racing super shoe that is lighter, faster, and more nimble. The standout feature is the 100% PEBA midsole paired with a carbon-infused PEBAX plate that strikes a perfect balance between a springy and stable ride. On smooth, flowy single track in Santa Barbara, CA, running in the Cascadia Elite felt almost effortless, and a ton of fun.

40 millimeters under the heel is a lot of foam to deal with, but the ride never felt squishy or overly bouncy in off-camber footing. A wide platform, paired with a flexible, embedded horseshoe-shaped plate, keeps the Cascadia Elite from being tippy. That width does come at a cost, though; picking tight lines through technical terrain requires precise footing to keep from getting wedged between rocks.

If you’re in the market for a trail running shoe, first consider the type of trails you run on regularly: do you tackle rugged, mountainous terrain, or stick to mellow dirt paths? Some trail shoes can handle both adequately, while others are specialized and excel in one or the other. Shoes with smaller lugs are generally better on smoother, firmer terrain, whereas shoes with deeper, more aggressive outsoles are optimized for steep, muddy, or rocky trails. If you like to feel the trail and dance around rocks and roots, you’ll likely prefer a light, more minimal shoe, but if you’d rather let the shoe roll over trail variations, cushioning and protecting while you zone out, you should look for a shoe with a thicker midsole.

Once you’ve narrowed the search to a certain type of trail shoe, you need to find a pair that complements your unique body and stride. Every runner’s body, gait, speed, experience, and ride preferences are different, so every runner will interact differently with each trail shoe. The shoe that your best friend or your sister-in-law loves may be uncomfortable for you and make running feel slow, sluggish, or even painful. Finding the perfect pair of trail running shoes is a seriously personal affair.

The process for choosing the best running shoes is a matter of finding the models that both fit your foot and also feel best when you’re running. To determine fit and feel, there’s no substitute for trying the shoes on and running in them.

When assessing fit, first pay attention to length. You need room at the end of your toes as your feet lengthen during their dynamic movements on the run. A rule of thumb is to allow a thumb’s width between your longest toe and the end of the shoe. Runners often wear a running shoe a half or full size bigger than their street shoes.

Ensure that the shape of the sole and the upper matches your foot shape. The sole should be as wide or wider than your foot for the whole length, and match the curve of your arch comfortably. The shoe should hold your foot securely over the instep, while allowing the ball of the foot and the toes to splay and flex when you roll forward onto them. Your heel shouldn’t slip when you lift it, and the arch should be able to dome and lengthen naturally. Nothing should bind or rub as you roll through the stride.

If the shoe fits, it’s time to take them on a short run on a treadmill, around the store, or, ideally, down the block and back. Every trail running shoe has a unique ride created by the type and density of foam in the midsole and the geometry of that foam: its thickness, width, heel-to-toe drop, molded sidewalls or flares, and forefoot flexibility or rocker shape (plus, in an increasing number of models, the presence of and type of embedded plate). Each of these elements interact with each other and your stride to determine how the shoe reacts on landing, how much it cushions, how stably it supports, how smoothly it transitions from landing to toe off, and how quickly and powerfully it rebounds.

The best way to choose trail running shoes that complement your body and stride is to find the ones that feel right on the run. Benno Nigg, the world-leading biomechanics professor who proposed this method of shoe selection, calls it the “comfort filter,” but makes clear it is far more than how plush the shoe feels when you step into it. What you want to assess is whether the shoe allows and supports the way your feet want to move, what Nigg calls your “preferred movement path.” In the right shoe, while running at your normal pace, you will touch down where you expect to land, roll smoothly and stably through the stride without noticing the shoe, feel both cushioned from and connected to the ground, and push off naturally, quickly, and powerfully. When this comes together you’ll know that you’ve found your pair.

It’s likely that several shoes will feel good on your feet. To find the most comfortable, it helps to compare them back to back, like an eye doctor will do with corrective lenses: flipping between “A” or “B,” “1” or “2.” You may also find that different shoes feel better at different paces or level of fatigue, and you may want more than one pair. In fact, research shows that wearing a variety of different shoes is one of the few proven ways to reduce injury risk as it appears to vary the stresses on your feet and joints.

Running shoes have long been marketed and sold as prescriptive devices to help runners stay healthy, but there is little scientific evidence correlating shoes, or any specific shoe properties—like cushioning or pronation control—with running injuries. Medical professionals say that it is highly difficult to determine whether a runner needs a certain type of shoe, and studies have shown that prescribing shoes using traditional methods like treadmill gait analyses or wet-foot arch height tests don’t consistently reduce injuries.

Don’t assume that you need more cushioning or more stability if you have sore joints, or if you’re a heavier runner, or if you’re a beginner—evidence doesn’t support many common beliefs. The best way prevent injury is find two or three different pairs that feel right on the run, ease into using them, and vary your shoes, your running surface and your pace regularly (plus avoid rapid increases in your training load and work on improving your mechanics).

Each season, we evaluate new releases from top outdoor brands, distributing samples to testers based on foot shape and local trail conditions and preferences. For this fall update, we evaluated 5 new models alongside 91 previously tested shoes to select the best trail running shoes on the market.

Over two to four months of testing on varied terrain across the country (from Santa Barbara to Boulder, Nebraska to New Hampshire), our team provided detailed feedback on fit, comfort, traction, cushioning, and responsiveness. We combined these reports with our own trail testing to select category winners and top recommendations for every type of runner.

Freelance journalist, editor, and author Lisa Jhung has researched, tested, and written about running shoes for the past decade and a half, much of that time for Outside. She coordinates a fleet of female shoe testers out of Boulder, Colorado, and says her home office is a perpetual obstacle course of cardboard boxes and piles of running shoes. Lisa’s written about gear of all kinds for numerous national magazines as both an editor and freelancer, including a stint as the shoes and gear blogger and trail running microsite editor for Runner’s World.

A high school jumper and occasional sprinter/hurdler, she started running—really running—after walking off the collegiate volleyball team, and moved on to road and trail races of any distance, triathlons, adventure races, and mountain running. She’s happiest testing rugged trail shoes on gnarly terrain, and also loves a good neighborhood jaunt…but is almost always looking for ribbons of dirt. Lisa is the author of Running That Doesn’t Suck: How to Love Running (Even if You Think You Hate It) and Trailhead: The Dirt on All Things Trail Running.

Cory’s passion for running started over 30 years ago in high school when he became the number six ranked runner in the nation at 3000 meters his senior year. After high school, he competed at Villanova University, earning two NCAA Division I Championship showings. Today, he’s determined not to let age slow him down and competes on the national master’s circuit, running a 4:12 (4:30 mile pace) 1500 meters and 9:04 (4:52 mile pace) 3000 meters in 2021 at age 43. He prefers a hard track workout or tempo run over an easy long run any day but also appreciates a challenging trail or mountain run.

His obsession with running shoes started in 2014 when he wrote his first shoe review for Gear Institute. Since then, he’s tested and reviewed hundreds of running shoes, clothing, and gear for Outside, Runner’s World, Footwear News, and other outlets. He has a soft spot for speedy shoes over heavy trainers but loves dissecting all shoes equally and thinking like a product engineer to explain the why behind every design detail. Cory is the Founder of Run Your Personal Best, an online running coaching business, and since its inception in 2014, has coached runners to over 100 Boston Marathon Qualifying times.

One of Cory Smith’s go-to routes for testing trail running shoes:

Jonathan fell in love with running his freshman year of high school and quickly became fascinated with finding the perfect pair of running shoes. That quest got a boost when he became editor of Running Times in 2000 and started receiving every new model as they were released. The parade of shoes continued while he served as shoe editor for Runner’s World, then editor of PodiumRunner, and currently fitness gear editor at Outside. Having now worn nearly every running shoe created in this century—and a fair amount of those dating back to the early models of the ’70s—he’s given up on finding the one best and now relishes the wide variety of excellent options.

Once a 2:46 marathoner regularly doing 50+ mile weeks, recent injuries and his age have reduced his volume and slowed his pace—but he still enjoys an uptempo workout or two each week. Beverly is the author of the book Your Best Stride which explores how each individual’s gait—and thus shoe preference—is unique. He enjoys getting scientists’ take on new shoe trends and trying to describe the nuances of each shoe’s ride.

#8310. The Best College Ski Towns in the U.S.

Big Sky and Lone Peak (Photo: Aerial_Views / Getty)

In today’s fast-paced, instant-gratification-obsessed world, it’s harder than ever for colleges to grab a young person’s attention. Don’t get us wrong, they’re trying, turning to drastic measures like on-campus waterparks, steakhouses, and even valet parking to attract a rising crop of future graduates.

But what if colleges had a taller, more natural card to play? For some mountain lovers, the idea of a college experience that combines curriculum with outdoor adventure is a prime way to push the needle. The prospect has made university towns like Burlington, Vermont, and Salt Lake City, Utah, into winter sports juggernauts, but it has also brought smaller towns into the discussion, putting them on the map and putting their universities on the “must apply” list.

So, what’s the best U.S. college town for skiing and snowboarding? We considered a handful of factors (proximity is just the start, after all) to find that answer, region by region. That means more than just the skiing itself, but also the culture, cuisine, and community that come along with it, making these mountain paradises appeal to college students and graduates alike. When it comes to studying hard and shredding harder, here are the best places to earn those turns…err, degrees.

The sheer amount of ski areas and college towns in the Northeast is enough to overwhelm, but let’s keep it simple: there’s only one Burlington, Vermont. Perched on the edge of Lake Champlain, this four-season wonder is also home base for the University of Vermont, St. Michael’s College, and Champlain College—and a whole lot of skiers and boarders between the three. In addition to national championship-winning alpine and Nordic ski programs, UVM has also grown one of the strongest ski and snowboard clubs in the country. Mountains around Burlington are all about showing their student population love, serving up heavily discounted college season passes at resorts like Jay Peak, Sugarbush, Mad River Glen (skiers only), and Smugglers’ Notch. The days of the legendary Triple Major may be over (if you know, you know), but there are still plenty of cheap turns for the higher education crowd.

After a long day on the slopes, take a walk down Church Street for the ultimate cultural contrast. This pedestrian-only brick walkway echoes Europe with a uniquely New England appeal. Stop at the Church Street Tavern for a local brew and then trek to Bove’s for its famous Italian cuisine. Burlington is a music hotbed, so don’t forget to pay your respects at Higher Ground on your way out of town.

Lake Champlain—need we say more? This large body of freshwater is Burlington’s lifeblood, providing public beaches, public sailing centers, unmatched paddling access, and even some fun urban cliff jumping (we suggest Red Rocks for an evening plunge). The Green Mountains earn their name here in the summer, crisscrossed with hiking and biking trails that rival most any in the country. Camel’s Hump might be the crown jewel, but there are plenty of day hikes within a short drive of town.

You might not think of the Southeast as ski country, but don’t tell Boone, North Carolina. This college town is home to Appalachian State University and set at the foot of the Blue Ridge Mountains—one of the premier snow-sliding regions in the South. Boone is an easy drive from three formidable Southeast ski resorts, and Appalachian Ski Mountain is less than 15 minutes from campus. In addition to having one of the best ski schools on the East Coast, the local area has night skiing and four terrain parks. On select nights throughout the season, students can score $16 night skiing tickets as well. For the more advanced, Beech Mountain is just 45 minutes away, opening up a realm of on-hill possibilities.

If you’ve made it out to Beech Mountain, don’t sleep on the 5506’ Skybar—the highest elevation bar on the Eastern Seaboard. For those looking for a lower elevation reward, the town of Boone is known for its home-crafted beer scene and beautiful downtown. Grab a pint at Appalachian Mountain Brewing or size up a mocktail at Fizzed before checking out Blowing Rock Village south of Boone’s downtown.

Boone was a summer escape long before it became a winter destination, once considered the finest vacation retreat between Newport, Rhode Island, and Palm Beach, Florida. Nowadays residents live the best of both worlds, scoring winter turns before hitting the summertime bike trails at Rocky Knob Mountain Bike Park. Fly-fishing aficionados have their pick of honey holes along the Blue Ridge Parkway and local guides are friendly enough to share the goods, or at least some of them.

Set smack dab in the middle of one of the country’s most overlooked snowbelts, Marquette, Michigan, has the distinct pleasure of being both off the tourist map and in the crosshairs of winter’s biggest storms. The largest city on Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, Marquette is also a university town, welcoming students to Northern Michigan University every fall. But when snow starts to fall, this student population converts to bona fide powder hounds. Marquette Mountain sits within city borders and receives over 210 inches a year—making it one of the snowiest places east of the Mississippi. NMU students get a whole season of it for just $361.

If just enjoying the slopes isn’t enough, undergrads can also pursue an associate degree in ski area management. This unique program runs in conjunction with Gogebic Community College, a school that places students into five-month internships at actual ski resorts and has its own ski hill, Mount Zion, right on campus.

Marquette is where college bar and ski bar collide into one heck of an après evening. Grab a $2 mystery beer at the Wooden Nickel Bar or dive into a face-sized cocktail while taking over the jukebox at Remie’s. The Midwest does après different—and we’re all for it.

Set on the shores of Lake Superior, Marquette turns students into long-term residents. Presque Isle Park and the Black Rocks offer up stunning, cliffside trails and wild forest, while biking in the NTN trail systems features a little something for every ability level. Cutting right through town, the Iron Ore Heritage Trail stretches 47 miles across the region, connecting caves, ruins, and historical stops related to the area’s mining roots.

This pick’s a little spicy, but hear us out. Boulder and Crested Butte have the skiing and mountain biking thing on lock. Salt Lake City has mountain proximity in spades. But Durango? This college town has a bit of everything—minus the people and mountain-bound bustle. Home to Fort Lewis College, Durango sits in the cradle of Colorado’s San Juan Mountains, an overlooked corner of the state with some serious vertical relief. Students attending Fort Lewis have their pick of Purgatory, Wolf Creek, and Hesperus within an hour or so of campus, but for those seeking bucket-list turns, Silverton and Telluride are a respectable day trip. If class is letting out late, there’s even Chapman Hill, a small (but steep) community ski area at the edge of campus, which offers an entire season of skiing and riding for $130.

Durango is a locals’ town right down to its libations. While several breweries have popped up over the years (Animas, Steamworks, and Ska, to name a few), it’s hard to pass up a post-mountain beer at Anarchy Brewing Co. Aside from some seriously strong IPAs (we liked the Sex Panther), this spot is four-legged friendly and has good food served on its outdoor patio.

If you just can’t wait to wet your whistle, the town’s biggest cheat code is the Durango Hot Springs Resort and Spa. It may sound bougie, but this series of naturally heated pools is a hangout that will soothe the soul without breaking the bank. The facility offers beer and wine for purchase and is only 20 minutes from Purgatory Ski Resort.

It’s deals and access like this that keep Durangatangs in town after they graduate, but while winter is a highlight, this locale is all about summer recreation. The Animas River runs right through the heart of Durango, often dotted with rafters and flotillas of varying sizes. Further downstream, the town has its very own whitewater park, and Durango Whitewater is a direct feeder program to the U.S. Olympic whitewater teams.

Beyond the river, Durango features hundreds of miles of mountain biking trails ranging from flowy beginner to some of the gnarliest technical terrain in the West. In fact, in 2030 the town is slated to host the UCI Mountain Bike World Championships.

Set between Montana’s two biggest mountain resorts and home to a robust network of in-town Nordic skiing, Bozeman has quietly been cultivating its ski community for decades. Students at Montana State University can take a free shuttle bus to nearby Bridger Bowl or unlock a discounted season pass at Big Sky (though it won’t include Saturdays or tram access). But Montana State skiers and snowboarders are not just on-piste enthusiasts. For the backcountry curious, the school has a strong backcountry scene including a dedicated Backcountry Club for avalanche education, gear help, group trips, and networking with professionals in the nearby Custer Gallatin National Forest and beyond.

It just so happens that some of Montana’s most epic skiing is located above some of Montana’s most epic après bars, so lucky you. Grab a pint at Scissor Bill’s in Big Sky or sip a Cold Smoke Scotch Ale at the Grizzly Bar off the Bridger Bowl parking lot—either way, you can’t lose.

The key to a good night is making it back to Bozeman, though, where Main Street offers up one of the more fun Eagles Club experiences around, complete with cheap drinks and rowdy live music. The Zebra is another community staple, where college students, ranchers, and old-timers can mingle over good local tunes.

Bozeman is an outdoors town with a frontier soul. The changing demographics lean toward outdoor recreation, but there’s an underlying and common current dedicated to protecting and enjoying the wild places in its periphery, and it shows. Hyalite Canyon is home to some of the best ice climbing in the world, and hosts a slew of climbers, runners, Nordic skiers, and hikers year-round. The Gallatin and Madison Rivers and Bozeman Creek all pass through or near town as well, giving anglers and kayakers primo access right out the front door, and plenty of options for anyone looking to play a little midweek hooky.

This Northwest representative was a close call with Bellingham and its coastal charm, but there’s something about the high desert that just doesn’t quit. Bend didn’t start out as a college town, but with the arrival of Oregon State University’s Cascade Campus (and the continued local support for Central Oregon Community College), this outdoors hotspot has become one heck of a diploma destination. Just 30 minutes from the 360-degree volcano skiing and riding of Mount Bachelor, Bend is a college town wrapped in mountain pedigree. We’d be silly not to mention the extensive backcountry access in Deschutes National Forest, and the Olympians that have come out of Mount Bachelor’s powerhouse Nordic skiing program. All of that and 300-plus sunny days a year? Where do we enroll?

Ski bar legend has it that before après was a French word, it was a guiding light in Central Oregon. Kidding aside, few ski towns have as many post-ski food and beverage options as the mighty Bend. While the boom has curbed in recent years, there are still over 30 breweries and taprooms within Bend city limits. Crux Fermentation Project and Monkless Belgian Ales rest on the banks of the picturesque Deschutes River, but the cozy climes and kickass beer at Terranaut Beer won Oregon’s Small Brewery of the Year in 2025.

For folks who turn college degrees into outdoor family roots, there are few spots quite like Bend. With year-round river recreation (including a retractable surf wave co-designed with surfer Gerry Lopez) and multiple trail running and mountain biking trail systems around town, Bend residents don’t know how or care to sit still. Beyond city limits, Central Oregon is an absolute natural playground, whether it be rock climbing and hiking around Smith Rock State Park, wandering the woods around Sisters, or getting out on the water in Prineville. If your friend says they’ve gotten bored of Bend, it’s time to find a new friend.

#8309. Great Hydration is About More than Just Electrolytes

Harmless Harvest shelf-stable coconut water. (Photo: Harmless Harvest)

Hydration comes up a lot when we talk about performance and recovery. Are you drinking enough water? Are you getting enough electrolytes? Are you tracking your fluid intake? It can be overwhelming to keep tabs of every statistic and ounce, but the hype around hydration isn’t without cause. Hydration is not only an essential component of pre-, mid- and post-workout performance. It’s an essential part of everyday life.

Electrolytes are a particular point of focus among performance athletes. Electrolytes are the minerals that help maintain the balance of fluids inside and outside your body’s cells. This is a critical consideration when it comes to high-exertion workouts where you’re losing lots of fluids through sweat.

The market is more saturated (pun intended) than ever with tablets, powders and pouches galore to help you optimize and maximize your electrolyte intake. But hydration doesn’t have to be as complicated as all that—and the conversation surrounding electrolytes doesn’t have to be reserved for elite athletes. It can be an everyday consideration for your morning walk, a quick out-and-back hike, or your daily commute to the office. And it all starts with a single coconut.

That’s the mission behind Harmless Harvest, a California-based company championing the coconut, turning a remarkable fruit into a remarkable lineup of products. It’s new pantry-friendly coconut water contains one ingredient: 100% coconut water with no added sugar or preservatives. The simplicity of their products ladder up to the simplicity of the brand’s philosophy—that great taste, quality ingredients, and premium tasting hydration should be for everyone to enjoy. Uncomplicated hydration doesn’t have to be a statistic for you to overanalyze—it can be an intentional and enjoyable part of your everyday life.

So what’s so great about a simple bottle of coconut water? Well, it’s just that: the simplicity. All on its own, coconut water delivers naturally occurring electrolytes, including potassium, to support everyday hydration. Unlike the formulated hydration drinks, tablets and powders that rely on added electrolytes, coconut water provides those muscle-supporting, fluid-balancing minerals into every bottle of Harmless Harvest coconut water naturally. Every bottle is made with a single ingredient with that naturally sweet coconut taste that’s completely delicious and refreshing.

From your pantry to wherever the day takes you, Harmless Harvest’s newest coconut water makes it easier than ever to keep great-tasting hydration close at hand. With no refrigeration required, you can keep bottles at room temperature until you’re ready to enjoy. Grab a bottle on the way to yoga, before a big day on the slopes, or just on the way to work. And unlike the traditional flash pasteurization commonly used by beverage producers, Harmless Harvest’s optimized heat treatment and micro-filtration preserves the fruit’s natural sweetness and nutrients, so you’re getting everything the mighty coconut has to offer.

Another question you might be asking is why is Harmless Harvest’s coconut water pink? Rather than using additives to control color variation from bottle to bottle, the company has embraced the pink hue that can come with the interaction between the coconut water’s antioxidants and natural elements like light and temperature.

Harmless Harvest’s commitment to sustainability and environmentally conscious practices extends beyond the bottle, too. The brand works with coconut growers in Thailand to source ethically farmed, non-GMO coconuts and also invests in initiatives that support farmers and their communities. These conscientious business practices aim to bring you products that you can sip with peace of mind.

Coconut water may not be the first thing you think to grab before a big workout or after a long run. It’s not a product that we typically associate with performance and recovery, but perhaps that’s the whole point. Don’t get us wrong, electrolytes are important, but in the age of optimization, where every mile, calorie and ounce of water is tracked, logged, and analyzed, it’s good to get back to the basics.

Being well-hydrated shouldn’t be reserved for when you’re pushing your body to its limits. Harmless Harvest’s mission is to show that just like general wellness, proper hydration goes beyond a numerical value—it’s about being mindful and listening to your body, one sip at a time.

Harmless Harvest creates delicious, premium coconut-based beverages and foods, crafted with care for people and the planet. Known for its naturally hydrating coconut water, the brand is committed to exceptional taste, responsibly sourced ingredients, and sustainable farming practices. Its mission is simple: make remarkable products while doing less harm and more good.

#8308. How Useful Is An Alpine Climbing Award, Really?

The Ultar Sar team, of Sebastian Pelletti, Ethan Berman, and Maarten Van Haeren, accept their Piolet d'Or in Saint-Christophe-En-Oisans, France, in October 2026. (Photo: Piotr Drożdż)

When I learned I’d be attending a gala for the “Oscars of Alpinism,” I made a note to pack formal clothes. The Piolets d’Or, or Golden Ice Axes, is a big deal; a rare career-building opportunity in a professional alpinist’s life. Earning this award can transform a strong amateur into a full-fledged member of global alpinism’s elite. This year, I joined the recipients who’d been coaxed out of their humble mountain hideouts to partake in alpinism’s biggest award ceremony.

Established in 1992, the Piolets have a respectable mission: to promote difficult, alpine-style new routes on the world’s great mountains. But the award has weathered plenty of criticism over the years. After rejecting his Piolet nomination in 2006, U.K. legend Ian Parnell later wrote in Alpinist: “Is it possible to choose a winner in an inherently unquantifiable pursuit [like alpinism]?” Others decry the Piolets d’Or for awarding climbers who recently died in the mountains, as well as for holding a subjective line of what counts as good climbing style.

I’ve been critical of the Piolets at times myself, especially after hearing one well-known alpinist talk longingly of wanting to climb something worthy of the award. I winced thinking about anyone tackling runout mixed terrain at high altitude with a golden ice axe taunting them overhead.

I thought of these critics, and my own biases, during my transatlantic flight a few weeks ago to this year’s ceremony in Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans, France. The award clearly has a dark side. But it has also become increasingly important in the year 2026. Lately, I’ve watched the professional climbing landscape bend to the pressures of sponsorship and social-media engagement—physical performance is but one metric to make a modern-day alpinist’s career.

In this new landscape, we see some climbers eager to make a quick buck. Others orient ascents around appeasing future sponsors or gaining attention online. In some instances, this materializes as full-scale fraud. In others, imaginative white lies of what constitutes a “summit.”

Through this lens, the Piolets d’Or represents an institution that is slowly becoming necessary. Nearly every year for the last 34 years, a varied, rotating cast of legendary alpinists sifts through the reams of new climbing achievements. Tossing aside marketing fluff and half-baked route attempts, they present to the world the year’s genuine highpoints of alpinism.

I wanted to know: Does the good of the Piolets d’Or outweigh the bad?

The singular Piolet d’Or first launched with the aim of recognizing the greatest alpine ascent of the previous year. In true Oscars’ fashion, at the early Piolet, all of the potential candidates were invited to an in-person ceremony, where the sole winner was read out, for the first time, in front of a couple thousand people.

“It was a mess,” British alpinist Paul Ramsden, one of this year’s jury members, told me of the Piolet’s early days. He and countryman Mick Fowler had been invited to the ceremony in Paris in 2003, when their ascent of Siguniang (6,250m) in China was in the running. “We all got up onto the stage, and they read my and Mick’s names out, and a French team beside us burst into tears,” Ramsden said.

American Dean Potter was on stage too, in the running for his solo ascents of the Patagonian spires Cerro Torre and Fitz Roy. When he got snubbed, he was livid, Ramsden remembered. Potter screamed at the organizers, asking why they’d told him to fly all the way to Europe to stand on stage for an award they knew he’d never receive.

Later that evening, in a sign of the early Piolet d’Or attitude, a special party took place offsite to celebrate Ramsden and Fowler’s win. With his golden ice axe in hand, Ramsden remembered ambling over to the afterparty, only to be stopped by a bouncer. The club had a dress code, and Ramsden was wearing sneakers. “So we weren’t allowed into our own party,” Ramsden laughed.

The Piolet d’Or ran uninterrupted from 1992 to 2007, when mounting criticism came to a head. Most notable was from the Slovenian alpinist Marko Prezelj, who was invited to that year’s event after his ascent of Chomo Lhari (7,326m), on the border of Tibet. He walked slowly onto the stage, took a long pause, then refused to accept his award, explaining why he thought the Piolet was antithetical to his view of alpinism. “Comparing different climbs is not possible without some kind of personal involvement and even then it is difficult,” Prezelj later wrote. “Last year I climbed in Alaska, Patagonia, and Tibet. I cannot decide which expedition was the most… the ‘most what’ in fact?”

Prezelj and others had become increasingly uneasy with how the Piolet d’Or pitted alpinists against each other. With only one winner, everyone else, in their eyes, became a loser. Such was not the spirit of alpinism.

The organizers cancelled the ceremony in 2008 and took a beat to reimagine it. A year later, after personnel changes and plenty of disagreements, a new version of the Piolet emerged, complete with an updated charter. The now-plural Piolets rewarded a climb’s lightweight style, self-sufficiency, technical difficulty, and management of objective hazards. Most importantly, though, the Piolets adopted a more community-based attitude. Everyone who was nominated for the award was given a Piolet d’Or.

This year’s ceremony was devoid of the drama that tainted the Piolet’s past. No one walked onto the stage just to reject the award. There was no French team in tears, and—as far as I could tell—no leery feeling of one-upsmanship among the award recipients. It was a bunch of climbers, wearing sneakers and duct-taped down jackets, drinking a bit too much red wine.

Paul Ramsden, who is 57, has been to a number of these week-long parties over the years, five times as a recipient—the most of any climber—and multiple times again as a jury member. Despite the criticism it’s received over the years, and his own jarring experience in 2003, he is now a proud supporter of the Piolets d’Or.

“I see awful style from climbers in some parts of the world,” he told me, citing large teams with bolt kits and hundreds of meters of fixed ropes, all but assured to succeed with enough dogged, industrial determination. “By rewarding alpine-style climbs, we’re not really rewarding the recipients. We’re signalling to the rest of the climbing community what ‘good’ style is.” In practice, that means that if a climber doesn’t have the skill to scale an unclimbed face with the same hardware they might take to a crag, they should leave the objective for a future generation of climbers who can.

One alpinist, who wished to remain anonymous, but has been nominated for a Piolet before, emphasized how flimsy and subjective any notion of “good” climbing style is. In a phone call with me, they noted how the Piolets jury considers climbing in insulated boots and ultralight crampons with Google-Earth reconnaissance as “good” climbing style, but considered carrying a few extra ropes to fix sections of the route poor form. The jury considers climbing in a lightweight team of two an enviable expression of alpine self sufficiency, yet a team of five or six is antiquated and ungainly.

Even understated, minimalist climbing expeditions to the Himalaya these days require a cottage-industry of resources: international flights, bus rides, porters, cook tents, tens of thousands of dollars of equipment—the list goes on. Deciding what the “correct” amount of resources an expedition should use is an inexact science, and one which the Piolets jury is still figuring out.

“I think it’s cool that we have a pretty objective governing body deciding what is actually good for alpine climbing,” Australian-Argentine climber Sebastian Pelletti, a recipient of a Piolet this year, told me. Like me, Pelletti has noticed professional alpinists erroneously claiming a “new” route to their sponsors and the world.

Last year, I wrote about one of those so-called new routes on Jirishanca (6,094m), in Peru’s Cordillera Huayhuash. Three very famous European alpinists climbed about a thousand meters of new terrain to the mountain’s summit ridge. Above, a spine of unconsolidated snow—the crux of the mountain—proved too difficult for the team. They bailed. A few days later, the climbers and their sponsors plastered a topo for this new route far and wide, drawing a bright red line that stopped on Jirishanca’s “east summit.” The east summit does not exist, nor has it ever been considered a final destination on the mountain. It is a brief bump in an otherwise vertical landscape, at least six pitches below Jirishanca’s actual summit.

When I wrote that article, some people called it a hit piece; I thought I was going light on the climbers. So when the Piolets d’Or announced their “long list” of notable ascents of 2025 earlier this year, I combed through it, seeing which routes made the cut. (Not all long-listed ascents are short-listed for the Piolets d’Or. The long list aims to recognize all new alpine climbs accomplished in good style.)

The Jirishanca “east summit” team was absent in the Peru section; the jury had not even considered their effort a route. But also within Peru’s long list, in the very same Huayhuash range, was a route on a mountain I had not heard much about, by climbers far less famous than their peers down valley. It was about the same length as the Jirishanca route, and just as difficult, but it went to the summit of Yerupajá Grande (6,635 m) and down the opposite side of the mountain. The climbers called it The Essence of Commitment, and they were being awarded the highest prize in alpinism.

#8307. My Favorite Spot in Denali National Park Is a Literal Pile of Trash

Old cans abound at one historic dump in Denali National Park. (Photo: Ryleigh Norgrove)

One of my favorite spots in Denali National Park’s vast wilderness isn’t some grand vista or rocky overlook. It’s much trashier than that.

Wander enough of the park’s frontcountry woods and you’ll come across all sorts of things: pioneer graves, little slate caves, mossy goshawk perches, a fantastic blueberry patch. Keep walking, and you might find a drainage as wide as a semi, full of garbage.

There are beer cans and glass bottles, coffee cans and broken gravy boats. It looks like a house disgorged its contents on a hillside and the tundra is slowly gobbling them up

The first time I encountered it, I wondered why no good Samaritan had come along with a bag or several by now, to haul this away to some other, less federally protected pit. We’re supposed to pack it out, after all.

After asking around at the local dive, I learned something else: This trash was considered historic. It felt like an oxymoron to me: How could a bunch of nasty empty beer cans tell us anything about the past other than a bunch of old-timers here liked to get drunk together, or that they were serving alcohol during prohibition?

One answer is that people don’t tend to write down what they’ve had for lunch. Or what kind of socks they wore through, or what they dropped and shattered. Discarded objects don’t mean much once they’ve hit the bin. And that’s exactly why impromptu landfills like this are one of the most significant sources of data archaeologists have.

“A lot of the stories of these individuals in the past never got written down,” says Dr. Justin Cramb, an assistant professor of archaeology at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, told me. “So the material traces are what we have.”

Archaeologists actually have a word for this historic trash: middens. They’re nasty and they’re everywhere. Depending on their age, they could contain shells, animal bones, or the last of someone’s canned dinner. They’re treasure troves of information, teaching us how people lived. Enough of them, alongside the other things people discarded, might tell you something about making a home in a place like Denali where getting groceries was considerably more complicated than driving to the store.

It’s something Cramb knows well. Throughout his work, he looks for details of daily lives: what resources people had, how they built their camps, and where they might have gathered building materials. Garbage is a part of that evidence.

“At the time, the world was kind of considered to be too vast to worry about those kind of things,” Cramb said. “And often in cases, somebody’s living at a place like Denali, they’re not going to haul their trash out, right? There was no mechanism for that to happen.”

Still, surely not every empty beer can deserves to spend eternity in a national park. But what’s the birthday on which it graduates from trash to treasured artifact?

The answer I got from the National Park Service on this was less tidy than I expected: “Age alone does not determine whether an object warrants preservation.”

It comes down to preserving cultural resources as much as natural ones. There are a few laws involved: Under the National Historic Preservation Act, historic areas generally need to be at least 50 years old and meet certain criteria for historical significance and integrity. The Archaeological Resources Protection Act also covers archaeological resources more than 100 years old that have cultural significance. Neither amounts to a blanket instruction to save every old can, but they do offer about 50 years of leeway on either end to determine if something is worth saving.

Cramb put it this way: “The house I grew up in is over 50 years old, right? But it’s not a historic property.”

Apparently, getting old and falling apart isn’t enough. The issue lies in what an object can teach us. Was it associated with a significant person or event? Could it fill in a piece of history we don’t know much about? And is enough of that evidence still there to make sense of it?

Around nearby Riley Creek, there’s quite a bit of history to make sense of. Before this was a place to order a latte or catch a bus, it was a place people lived. On Thanksgiving Day, 1921, Maurice Morino opened his Mount McKinley Park Hotel to feed and entertain miners, trappers and travelers. Just down the road, there were cabins, a trading post, and a silver fox ranch. Down below the old railroad bridge, you could visit “the Hole” for gambling, bootlegging, and other activities you won’t find on the ranger-program schedule.

Later on, in 1932, the park boundary absorbed that community. Today, cabin remains, debris, and trash dumps are among the traces of McKinley Station. Morino’s grave is still here, too. I haven’t been able to trace who exactly left behind my little trash pile, but it’s tucked into a landscape with considerably more human history than the trees let on.

Of course, I’d left an imprint getting there, too. I’d followed one of those little paths through the woods and added my footsteps to the record. Even my wandering had inherited a shape.

There’s something difficult in that. I want to know these woods well enough to return to the blueberries when they’re ripe, to recognize the perch before I look up for the bird. That kind of knowing takes effort. But each one presses a little more of a path into the ground.

“I always say that the goal is really to leave as little trace as possible,” says Erin Collier, Director of Education for Leave No Trace. “That doesn’t sound as good, you know, on the T-shirt and on the logo, but that’s really what the goal is.”

“If we were truly leaving no trace,” she says, “we wouldn’t be out there.”

We leave evidence of ourselves just by visiting. Roads, campgrounds, the little paths we wear into the woods. The trick is in paying attention to what we’re adding, and what we might accidentally take away.

Sometimes that means resisting the urge to clean up. The Park Service advises leaving potentially historic objects exactly where they are and asking staff if you’re unsure. Where something lies, among the other things people left behind, is part of its story.

But that doesn’t give the rest of us permission to start contributing.

“Today we have the infrastructure to deal with things like taking our trash out of the park,” Cramb told me. “We can do better. So we should.”

I know these woods, and knowing them means accepting that other people have known them, too. Their lives are still here, in cabin foundations and coffee cans, slowly disappearing into the hillside. My own footprints will leave something behind. I’d like to be thoughtful about what that is.

This story grew out of Ryleigh’s Certified Interpretive Guide (CIG) coursework, taught by Suzanne Miller, Interpretive Programs Manager for the Doyon/Aramark Joint Venture at Denali National Park and Preserve.

#8306. The Rules of Trail Running Etiquette, from the ATRA President

As the president of the American Trail Running Association (ATRA)—a title that sounds more impressive than it is—and co-author of The Ultimate Guide to Trail Running,” which is now in its third edition, I know a little about the proper behavior of trail runners. And as a six-decade trail veteran myself, I also know a little about the improper behavior of trail runners.

To me, the “rules” of trail running are quite simple and boil down to two principles: respect nature, and respect other users.

Those two tenets blossom into about 10 “strong suggestions” for sustainable, copasetic trail experiences, but, like with the Golden Rule, it all comes down to showing respect. Here are the basics of what you should know when you hit the trails:

Close any gates you open, don’t disturb the wildlife or livestock, and respect private land and get permission to enter.

Take only photos and pack out at least as much as you brought in, including gel wrappers. If needed, wear shorts, a jacket, or hydration pack with zip pockets to stow rubbish found on the trail.

Don’t disturb wildlife as frightened animals may be dangerous. Steer clear of trails that disturb sensitive habitats during nesting or mating seasons. When passing horses, use special care and follow directions from the horseback riders. Consider turning around and going another direction when faced with large herds of animals.

Don’t play your music loudly, engage in boisterous conversations with your fellow runners (or through speakerphone), or listen to headphones so loudly that you are unaware of your surroundings. Along the same lines, do your social media influencing elsewhere. Nature is not your recording studio. We don’t want to hear you, and you ought to be able to hear others.

We expect the same of cyclists. This should be obvious but, then again, all of this should be.

As trail runners, we move relatively quickly, especially when we seemingly emerge from nowhere on unsuspecting trail users. This may be alarming, so anticipate and give a courteous and audible announcement of your presence and intention to pass hikers on the trail by stating something along the lines of, “On your left,” or “Trail,” as you approach. Keep an eye out for those wearing headphones, as they won’t hear your warning. Be courteous when passing, slowing down or stopping if necessary to prevent accidental contact. Be ready to yield to all other trail users (cyclists, hikers, horses) even if you have the posted right of way.

This is likely to be controversial, but consider not bringing your dog on group runs and, when you do run with your dogs, be sure to leash them and keep them under your control when necessary to prevent any wildlife disturbances. Be sure to pack out their (and your) waste.

Be cognizant that off-leash dogs often chase wildlife and degrade the outdoor experience of other trail users.

Greet and say “Excuse me” to those you see and pass on the trail. This should be a common practice if for no other reason than to alert others to your presence and not frighten anyone. Similarly, be sure to stay in control of your speed, especially when you could cause rocks or other trail features to fall.

If you startle someone, apologize, and thank them if they’ve stepped aside. A little kindness goes a long way on the trail.

Don’t cut the switchbacks or widen trails by running around puddles,downed trees, or when it is too muddy

Don’t create your own trails by running off preexisting, well-marked trails. When multiple trails exist, run on the most worn. Stay off closed trails and obey all postings.

Run single file in the middle of a trail, even if it’s laden with a fresh blanket of snow or thick mud. Go over, not around, obstacles like puddles,rocks, or downed tree limbs, as that widens trails, damages vegetation, and causes unnecessary erosion.

In other words, participate in trail maintenance and give back to the trail community.

In a now-infamous Outside opinion piece of seven years ago that went viral, Marc Peruzzi claimed that trail runners are lazy parasites. Ultrarunner and lawyer Stephanie Case wrote a response piece, saying more could be done, agreeing with my stance that “we are guilty as charged … we need [to do] more. A lot more.” Case continued, “Indeed, as trail running continues to increase in popularity, it will become even more important that we expand our volunteer and conservation efforts.”

So, carry your weight and do trail work. Volunteer. Go plogging on your local trails.

Technically, those ascending are supposed to have the right of way but, in practice, people often yield to descenders, likely due to speed and momentum. Be polite, maintain control, and be prepared to yield to other users, including horseback riders.

Split larger groups into smaller groups as bigger numbers can intimidate other users and have a greater environmental impact on trails.

If you come across someone in distress, stop and check whether they need help.

Don’t become a liability by taking risks, getting lost, or ignoring trail closures that require dangerous rescues. Carry proper clothing, nutrition, and hydration so as not to put yourself at risk of exposure. Safety first is always a good rule.

If running alone, familiarize yourself with the area where you plan to run and let at least one other person know your intended route. Be prepared for the weather and conditions when you start your run and plan for the worst, given the likely duration of your run. Know and respect your limits and report unsafe conditions and activities to the proper authorities.

Trail running is beautifully simple. So is being a courteous trail runner. Follow these tips for proper etiquette and keep the trails safe, welcoming, and wild!

#8305. New Research Shows How Much Altitude Actually Slows You Down

One of the all-time great topics for discussion on the Sunday long run is “What was so-and-so’s race performance really worth?” Andreas Almgren, for example, won this year’s New York Marathon by running the first half in 1:04:04 and the second half, including the hills of Central Park, in 1:01:57. What could he have run with a flatter course and more even pacing? Similarly, you can ponder the effects of factors like heat, wind, drafting, shoe design… and altitude.

Everyone understands that the thin air at high altitudes matters when you’re climbing Mount Everest, or even playing football in Denver. But the effects can also show up at much lower altitudes. I once spent a few months in Australia’s capital city, Canberra, which is only around 1,900 feet above sea level. I had a streak of disappointing road races—which only made sense once I realized that even at that altitude VO2 max is reduced by about five percent. Australian sports scientists had figured that out when they were setting up the Australian Institute of Sport in Canberra and noticed that their fancy new testing equipment seemed to produce abnormally low values.

This intrinsic worth of high-altitude performances is currently a hot topic because the NCAA voted over the summer to eliminate its altitude conversions for track and field qualifying standards. Until now, any performance at more than 3,000 feet above sea level was adjusted to account for the effects of less air resistance and lower oxygen levels. Sprint performances had time added, because thin air makes them faster; middle- and long-distance performances had time deducted, because the lack of oxygen made them slower.

The conversions were eliminated in part because, as the rules committee wrote, “there is no true science being applied” in formulating them. That makes a new study in the International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance slightly late to the party—but it’s interesting nonetheless. Atle Guttormsen and Simen Guttormsen of the Norwegian University of Life Sciences analyzed more than 900,000 individual performances from track meets at 382 NCAA indoor track venues over a 14-year period to determine exactly how much difference altitude makes.

The statistical analysis attempted to account for as many sources of variation as possible: the design of the track (e.g. banked or unbanked), how a given performance compared to the athlete’s other performances that season, how early or late in the season it was, and so on. (Conveniently, there’s no wind indoors.) Overall, they came up with an estimate for how much altitude affected various events per 1,000 meters of altitude (which is 3,281 feet).

Here’s the resulting data for six running events:

Up to 400 meters, athletes are faster at altitude. The effect at 60 meters is slightly smaller because (I’m assuming) they spend a large fraction of the race accelerating to top speed. At 200 meters, they’re about 0.4 to 0.5 percent faster than they would be at sea level. In the long jump, triple jump, and pole vault, all of which are speed-based (but not shown above), there’s a similar advantage.

The crossover, where lack of oxygen begins to outweigh lower aerodynamic drag, happens at race distances just beyond 400 meters. The negative effects of altitude climb steeply at distances of up to 3,000 meters, then level off. That’s because in these longer events, aerodynamic drag is mostly irrelevant, so the effects of altitude are purely negative. For distances of 3,000 meters and beyond, the negative effects of altitude in this dataset seem to be about 2.7 percent for every 1,000 meters of altitude. Note that 1,000 meters is just slightly more than 3,000 feet, where the NCAA’s altitude conversions used to kick in. That equates to a roughly 30-second disadvantage for 5,000-meter runners.

The most interesting point in this graph is the 800-meter data. Women experience a greater disadvantage than men at altitude: 0.92 percent versus 0.50 percent. Top NCAA men are running about 1:45, while top women are running about 2:00. Since they’re so close to the point where oxygen and aerodynamics balance out, that 15-second difference matters. The men are going faster, so they benefit more from the reduction in drag; the women are running for longer, so they suffer more from the lack of oxygen. The Guttormsens argue that the NCAA needs sex-specific conversion factors—but the argument is moot since the conversion factors have been scrapped, at least for now.

Assuming the oxygen-related penalty stays roughly constant at 2.7 percent beyond 3,000 meters, here’s what kind of slowdown you can expect in endurance events at various elevations:

The upshot: I can now tell myself that I was about 1.6 percent fitter than my half-marathon times in Canberra suggested. (I’ve been saying that for years anyway… but now I’ve got science!)

The problem is that altitude affects everyone differently. A few years ago, I wrote about a neat study showing that altitude-born South American cyclists perform relatively better in high-altitude race stages than European cyclists. Even though the Europeans were doing lots of altitude training camps, they couldn’t overcome the disadvantage of being born near sea level. Altitude response depends on a mix of genetics (where your ancestors lived), environment (where you live and/or train), and developmental factors (where you were born and grew up). This is another reason the NCAA cited in scrapping altitude conversion factors: the “right” conversion is different for everyone.

There’s even some evidence that trained endurance athletes are more susceptible to the negative effects of altitude than untrained people. That may be because their hearts pump blood so powerfully that it rushes past the lungs too quickly to pick up a full load of oxygen. This affects some athletes even at sea level, but becomes increasingly common as you climb in elevation.

Personally, Canberra isn’t the only history I’d like to revise: some of the most disappointing races of my life took place in Calgary (3,428 feet) and Edmonton (2,116 feet). These aren’t cities that anyone thinks of as “high-altitude,” but it’s clear that their elevation does have an effect—and that effect is bigger if you don’t realize that it exists, because in trying to stick with your expected pace you can burn yourself out early in the race. Knowing about these effects matters, and the new data gives you a starting point to make adjustments next time you head to the mountains—or even just the foothills.

For more Sweat Science, sign up for the email newsletter and check out my new book The Explorer’s Gene: Why We Seek Big Challenges, New Flavors, and the Blank Spots on the Map.

#8302. Colorado Trail and Continental Divide Trail ‘Extensively Damaged’ After Severe Flooding: Here’s What We Know

This article was updated on November 11, 2026, at 8:35 a.m. with additional information regarding the condition of the Colorado Trail section 28.

In just over a week, two massive flooding events hit southwestern Colorado, destroying homes, businesses, and infrastructure across numerous mountain towns. But property is not all that the floods affected. Parts of both the Continental Divide Trail (CDT) and the Colorado Trail (CT) suffered damage that locals and trail organizations are calling “extensive” and “severe”, and which could take a very long time to repair.

“Rebuilding these damaged sections will not be quick, easy, or cheap,” Paul Talley, executive director of the Colorado Trail Foundation (CTF), said in a November 5 update on the floods. “But we are committed to rebuilding.”

As many of these areas are still inaccessible, there is very little confirmed information on their current state. Videos circulating online show missing bridges at key river crossings, and reports from the USFS and other agencies indicate that trailheads are damaged, and “heavy debris” is blocking some sections. But there has yet to be a full, official report on damage to these trails.

Here is what we know so far based on official updates, local reports, and videos.

Junction Creek is the CT’s southernmost section. Its trailhead, just outside of Durango, is also the CT’s southern terminus. Junction Creek Trail crosses multiple footbridges over the creek along its 19-mile stretch. A conditions report on the U.S. Forest Service webpage says that a “Huge rock and heavy debris” is currently blocking the trail about a half-mile from the trailhead. One video claims to show an area along Junction Creek Trail near Gudy’s Rest, where a footbridge has been washed away completely. The USFS posted its own video of the road to Junction Creek to Facebook, showing a new “20-foot waterfall” over the edge of the destroyed road.

“There is no doubt that trails across the forest have suffered severe damage,” the San Juan National Forest wrote. “For example, we know that the Colorado Trail along Junction Creek has largely been obliterated and that the trail bridge is gone. In some sections, the trail is buried underneath riverflow that was re-routed during the flooding.”

On November 10, a Facebook user posted to the Durango Area Trail Conditions Report Facebook page with information about the trail section above Junction Creek. According to the report and accompanying photos, the Walls Gulch Bridge was destroyed, and the trail following Flagler Fork Creek sustained “major damage.”

Authorities said that recovery work would likely not begin until spring and summer 2027 due to weather, and discouraged hikers from even attempting to set out on the area’s trails.

“Record flooding across Southwest Colorado has left San Juan National Forest roads, trails, and other infrastructure inaccessible, severely damaged, and, in many cases, impassable,” another post reads. “Don’t become a statistic — rescue will not be readily available due to the current demand for search and rescue services.”

Another video posted to Instagram shows the sign that many hikers use for their CT terminus photo now standing directly at the edge of a tall wash filled with flood debris.

The CTF said that it will be working over the winter with USFS, local partners, and volunteers to determine timelines and project budgets for the restoration efforts.

“It will be months before we can better understand what the next steps need to be on the sections damaged by climate events this season,” wrote Talley in his November 5 update.

There is even less information regarding damage to the CDT, which also passes through the flood-affected areas of Southwestern Colorado.

The Continental Divide Trail Coalition (CDTC) posted on Facebook on October 23, warning hikers that flooding had made “travel to and from the CDT trailhead at Wolf Creek Pass impossible,” and that “hikers may need to make alternate plans to avoid the area.”

On November 2, the CDTC posted another update for CDT travelers. “The extent of damage to the CDT, access roads, and CDT communities is still unknown,” it said. While the interactive map on its website shows no current closures of the trail due to flooding, the CDTC advised hikers to use “extreme caution and check with local authorities before visiting.”

Backpacker reached out to the CDTC for comment, but did not receive a response by the time of publication.

While the full extent of the damage to these trails remains to be seen, what’s certain is that the CTF, CDTC, USFS, and other state agencies have a great deal of restoration work to do next summer. Volunteers will be in high demand, and Talley, of the CTF, promised to be open about how hikers can help.

“While we do not yet know what it will take to rebuild, we do know what we will need,” Talley wrote. “We will need our supporters, we will need our dedicated volunteers, and we will need that community spirit that makes the CT so special.”

#8299. Three Ground Rules for Getting Outside

Getting outside is for everyone. That’s what Sierra is all about, finding top active and outdoor brands at prices that make it accessible to try a bunch of new adventures. That’s the spirit behind Sierra in the Sierras, in which Dylan Efron (Emmy-winning co-producer of Netflix’s Down to Earth with Zac Efron) hits the trail with a friend to try something completely new.

With gear and apparel from Sierra and guidance from Outside editors, in episode one Dylan explores the Sierra Nevada with Danielle Fishel, Boy Meets World icon and Dancing With the Stars co-star. Whether it’s your first hike or just your first hike today, no one likes to be uncomfortable. The right gear helps. If you’re like Danielle, a self-proclaimed “indoor person,” or simply trying a new activity, you’ll want to focus on comfort and versatility above all else. The aim is to A) feel good while enjoying your new hobby and B) have the freedom to explore further as you progress. The gear choices at Sierra make this easy, thanks to a combo of trusted brands, great prices, and an ever evolving inventory of fresh finds in-store and online.
