#8284. The Historic SS United States Was Sunk off Florida to Become the World’s Largest Artificial Reef

SS United States (Photo: Destin-Fort Walton Beach)

As it turns out, it takes a lot to sink a 990-foot ocean liner.

The SS United States was supposed to start going down at 1 p.m. Central Time on Wednesday, November 11. Last-minute preparations pushed that to nearly 5 p.m. By 4:45, every valve was open, and the Gulf was pouring in. Then came four more hours of watching a ship refuse to leave. She finally slipped under at 8:59 P.M., twenty-two nautical miles southwest of Destin, Florida, in the Gulf of Mexico, tilting hard to her port side.

From a nearby boat, I watched the fastest ocean liner ever built make the slowest exit imaginable. On her maiden voyage in 1952, she beat the Queen Mary’s record by about ten hours. On Veterans Day, the iconic ocean liner needed about four hours just to go under.

With this scuttling—a deliberate, controlled sinking—the SS United States becomes the world’s largest artificial reef, surpassing the USS Oriskany, which had held the title since its 2006 sinking. It’s a second life that’s part habitat project and part tourism bet, and it follows years of failed rescue plans and a last-minute court fight.

Here’s how a ship once meant to become a museum ended up on the Gulf floor, what it means for the sea around her, and what divers can expect when they finally get to explore her underwater.

Why sink her off the Florida Panhandle? Habitat and tourism. The seafloor off Destin and Fort Walton Beach is mostly sand and shell, and natural reef is scarce. Okaloosa County’s tourism department laid out a five-year, $12 million plan to make Destin-Fort Walton Beach the dive capital of Florida, with part of the money coming from tourist-development tax revenue. Visit Pensacola and the Coastal Conservation Association’s Florida chapter signed on as partners. Part of that money funds a multiyear marketing campaign to promote the ship as a diving destination.

The SS United States is also slated to join the Florida Panhandle Shipwreck Trail. The state created the trail in 2012 to stimulate tourism, after the Deepwater Horizon oil spill. It began with twelve wrecks off Pensacola, Destin, Panama City, and Port St. Joe and has since grown to more than 20. Divers collect passport stickers at each one. These 20 ships are among 48 large vessels sunk by the county since the 1970s.

The SS United States now rests in about 180 feet of water. If she landed upright, as early sonar scanning indicates, her upper decks are roughly 50 to 60 feet down. The county says divers of all skill levels can reach the upper decks.

While there were once dreams of converting the 990-foot icon into a hotel or museum, she deteriorated to the point that the options came down to the scrapyard or an artificial reef.

The liner was abruptly withdrawn from service in 1969. She later spent nearly thirty years docked in Philadelphia, where no one managed to repurpose her.

For decades, owners kept hunting for the ship’s second act. In 2016, Crystal Cruises studied a return to sea and called the obstacles insurmountable. By the time a rent fight got the historic ship ordered off a Philadelphia pier in 2024, the nonprofit that owned the vessel says it was left with two options: scrap or “reef her”. Preservationists argue a museum ship was still possible.

The conservancy ultimately sold the liner to Okaloosa County, Florida, for $1 million. The county has spent a total of more than $13 million getting it ready to scuttle—remediation, towing, insurance, deployment—and contributing toward the yet-to-be-constructed museum dedicated to the ocean liner. The county’s tourism director calls the project an economic development opportunity and an environmental asset. Its tourism director told NPR the county expects to make back its investment in a couple of years.

A last-minute lawsuit nearly stopped the sinking. The SS United States Preservation Foundation sued the Army Corps of Engineers in federal court in Pensacola on November  3, arguing the agency failed to adequately weigh the ship’s toxic coatings under federal environmental law. Three days later, a judge denied the emergency request to halt the sinking, citing the lack of an affidavit and the cost of an injunction. An earlier suit from a separate New York group had already been dismissed in 2025.

On the whole, scuttling (or initially sinking) a properly cleaned vessel can house a new ecosystem for fish and other oceanic life. Crews drained and cleaned the fuel tanks of the SS United States, and no explosives were used. The county says it removed 99 percent of the PCB-containing materials, though nobody outside the project has independently verified that number.

The open question is the old zinc-chromate primer, which contains hexavalent chromium. Those who still wanted the ship preserved topside say it will leach. The county says it converts underwater into a less toxic form. A Drexel oceanographer called the risk “a little overblown,” while saying he’d still prefer mitigation. The Oriskany, another purpose-sunk vessel off the coast of Destin, which held the title of world’s largest artificial reef until Wednesday is a cautionary precedent. It became a thriving reef, but monitoring also found elevated PCBs in some of its fish.

Algae, barnacles, and sponges settle on the steel first. Corals can follow, then small fish, then the predators that hunt them. Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution is tracking the process at about 132 tagged spots on the wreck, with a goal of acquiring ten years of data.

Scientists still argue about whether reefs create new fish or just concentrate existing ones for anglers. Gulf red snapper research leans toward creation, though it comes mostly from oil platforms and smaller reefs, not one giant ship.

One more caveat: this is new habitat, not restoration. It was sunk in an area that was mostly sand, so no existing reef habitat was disturbed or restored. This is a net-new ecosystem for the region.

The iconic ship’s two sixty-five-foot funnels, propeller, and radar mast are headed to a land-based museum near Destin. Everything else now belongs to the Gulf.

Like the other divers who attended the sinking, I was hoping to dive it within the first 24 hours. But the rough conditions forecast for today, which pushed the sinking up one day, also kept us out of the water. I’ll be back as soon as I can to skim above the deck, but the bragging rights for the vessel’s first recreational dive are still up for grabs.

The exact date divers will have access to the new dive site is still unknown. Safety divers must clear the site before recreational divers are allowed.

Local charter operators are hoping to head out as soon as Friday. Niuhi Dive Charters says divers from all over the world have already signed up.

The county says her top deck, anticipated to be at 55 to 60 feet, is accessible to all levels of certified divers, which makes an Open Water certification the entry ticket. If you want more than a look at the top, Advanced Open Water, with its 100-foot-limit, is the better choice, and charter operators set their own requirements. Wreck and Nitrox certifications are smart additions. The lower decks belong to technical divers with decompression and trimix training.

Plan on a full day offshore. She’s about twenty-two nautical miles southwest of Destin-Fort Walton Beach, and Destin is the closest launch point. Divers can book through Niuhi Dive Charters or ScubaTech Destin, which runs daily Gulf charters aboard the Sea Cobra.

Alexandra Gillespie is the former digital editor of Scuba Diving magazine. With nearly 200 dives under her weight belt, and has covered scuba diving and marine sustainability for Outside, National Geographic, U.S. News and World, NPR, BBC, and other major publications. She’s gone diving everywhere from California’s kelp forests to Bahamian reefs to Sudan’s Red Sea.

#8283. This New Book Strives to Help Climbers Rewire Their Mental Game

(Photo: Left: Sam Douglas Jones / Right: Vertebrate Publishing)

We all do it: Eyeing other climbers and comparing ourselves to them. Wishing we were better at dynos, heel hooks, or some other elusive climbing move. Loading ourselves with shoulds when it comes to training or grades.

Even non-performance-oriented climbers like me tend to be guilty of at least some negative thoughts when we’re up on the wall. It’s hard not to think that way when so many highly specific levels dominate the sport. This makes the idea of progression almost impossible to resist, even if you claim to do it only for fun.

There is something about the progress ladder of the Yosemite Decimal System. Its slash grades, letter addendums, and pluses and minuses tempt you to try and tick routes with higher grades. The same goes for the V-scale, as well as many other grading scales. We often ask “What if?” questions about breaking into a harder grade. And we often define ourselves by the grades we climb. “I’m a V10 boulderer,” someone might say, or “I’m a 5.10 climber.”

Meanwhile, when I’m skiing or mountain biking, there are essentially only four, color-coded levels, green through double black. Compared to climbing, I find it rare for someone to ask what color run I skied or trail I rode—and did I make it down without falling? But after someone climbs a route, one of the first questions might be what the grade was. And did you send it?

As the sport continues to grow, two British climbers have noticed that the expansion of training content has far outpaced the rise of mindset content when it comes to climbing. And they agree that climbing tends to be uniquely progress-oriented compared to other sports.

“It’s great to see the growth in top-end performance climbing, but for a lot of people, that might come with a lot of pressure to perform the same way,” says Louis Parkinson, the founder of the coaching company Catalyst Climbing, a climber of over 20 years, and co-author of the new book Get a Grip.

To write a self-help book for climbers focused exclusively on mindset, Parkinson teamed up with Joel Robertson, an MA MBACP psychotherapist and climber. Nicknamed “The Climbing Therapist,” Robertson insists that their book isn’t only for elite or performance-oriented athletes. That’s because he believes climbers at any level can experience the pressure and negative thought patterns that the sport can induce. He also sees negative mentality extending beyond the sport.

“If you’re being brutal to yourself at the crag or in the gym in ways that are holding you back in climbing, then you’re almost certainly doing that to yourself at family Christmas or at work or whatever,” Robertson says. “Mental health and climbing mindset are not separate, right? Let’s treat them the same. That’s the whole ethos of the book.”

Both Parkinson and Robertson admit that they are far from perfect when it comes to their own mentality. They emphasize that a healthy climbing mindset requires continuous work, rather than a one-time solution.

A former competitive climber, Parkinson recalls a period where he stopped enjoying climbing. This triggered an identity crisis of sorts, since he had oriented his entire life and career around the sport. “If I stop climbing, then I don’t know who I am,” Parkinson recalls thinking.

Eventually, Parkinson realized that his lack of enjoyment stemmed from the immense pressure he was putting on himself to continuously improve. When he couldn’t perform up to his own standards, he became “really, really upset.” Once he eased off the unrealistic expectations he was holding himself too, the joy came back. Parkinson’s past struggle echoes a similar experience of Chris Sharma. Earlier this year, he talked with Climbing about letting go of grades in order to send Biographie, the world’s first 5.15.

Robertson, primarily a casual indoor boulderer, shares a more recent experience from a couple weeks ago. After three sessions, he flashed his gym project. In the midst of some celebratory fist pumps, however, he watched in mild horror as someone else came and flashed his project as their warm-up. “It’s so classic,” Robertson says of this common climbing predicament. “I genuinely felt way less good about the achievement and not just the achievement, but myself.”

To avoid comparing yourself to others in a negative way, one suggestion Get a Grip offers is to think about your climbing friends. Do you love and value them because of their climbing ability, or because of who they are? Most people care about each of their friends as a person, not in terms of their climbing abilities. When you start to compare yourself to others, or base your self-worth on whether you, for example, sent your project, try to view yourself as you would your friend instead.

Robertson and Parkinson also suggest focusing on comparisons that are accurate and valuable, rather than grounded in envy or self-pity. Instead of thinking, “Damn, I wish I could climb like that,” ask, “What could I learn from watching someone else that I could apply in my own climbing?”

One of the critical ways to work on climbing mindset is to cultivate more awareness around our own thoughts, according to Robertson and Parkinson. Rather than becoming bogged down in the thought, attempt to view the thought impartially. Try reframing the thought, or compartmentalizing it. “Rather than ‘I am anxious,’ it’s ‘a part of me is anxious,’” Robertson explains. This can help you get some distance between yourself and a fleeting notion or emotion.

Throughout the book, reflections from pro climbers bring more color and insight to what a strong mindset looks like. In one of my favorite sections, British boulderer and competitive climber Shauna Coxsey talks about asking questions instead of making statements. An “exploratory mindset,” as Robertson and Parkinson term it, will fuel you with curiosity rather than pressure. “People often think I’m a very motivated person, but I would disagree,” Coxsey writes after sharing her focus on curiosity. “I think I’m a very committed person. For me, motivation and commitment have to go hand in hand because it’s impossible to be motivated all the time.”

Another standout pro mindset cameo comes from another British boulderer and comp climber: Hamish McArthur. Essentially, he reveals that he more or less blacks out when he climbs hard. This allows him to enter the coveted flow state that so many of us seek. “The times when I’ve performed at my best, I don’t really have any memory of what it was like,” he writes.

I took a lot away from the book in terms of how to edit and take control of my internal monologue. But I was left with one nagging question: How can we all climb more like McArthur, and find that elusive flow state?

“Just think less. It’s easy!” Parkinson joked with me. “No, it’s really hard. It’s insanely difficult.” Parkinson clarifies that achieving a mindset like McArthur’s requires a long-term commitment to honing your meditation skills so you can quiet your mind and just climb. But the lessons in Get a Grip can help get you started.

Vertebrate Publishing released Get a Grip on October 8. You can find a copy from Catalyst Climbing, Amazon, and wherever books are sold. Climbers can also listen to Get a Grip as an audiobook narrated by Parkinson.

#8280. Georgia’s Entire 78-Mile Appalachian Trail Section Will Require Bear Canisters in 2027

A hiker carries a bear canister on the Appalachian Trail. (Photo: Courtesy Appalachian Trail Conservancy)

Hikers on Georgia’s stretch of the Appalachian Trail will need to store their food in a hard-sided canister next year according to a new order from the U.S. Forest Service, a change that follows years of rising bear encounters on the southern miles of the AT.

In a press release, the USFS said that the rule would take effect January 1, and would apply to anyone camping in a 1-mile-wide corridor along the entire 78-mile section of the AT, including hikers staying in shelters. The requirement is year-round and also applies to the AT Approach Trail.

Alternative food-storage methods like bear hangs and Ursacks will not be allowed. Hikers who violate the order could face a fine of up to $5,000 or 6 months in jail.

“With the Appalachian Trail going through the heart of North Georgia’s black bear habitat, we want the hikers who flock here to understand how incredibly valuable these public lands are—for people and for wildlife,” Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest Supervisor Judy Toppins said. “Finding a balance that protects hikers, wildlife, and forest health is our goal.”

As visitation to the Appalachian Trail has risen in recent years, human-bear conflicts have too, with a 2025 survey by the Appalachian Trail Conservancy finding that bear reports had risen by 75 percent that year alone. A disproportionate amount of those run-ins happen in Georgia: Morgan Sommerville, the ATC’s director of visitor use management, said that while just 3.5 percent of the AT lies in Georgia, the state accounted for more than 12 percent of its bear encounters.

The new requirements represent the largest expansion of food storage rules on the trail yet. Previously, only a few short segments required a canister, such as the 5-mile segment between Jarrard and Neel Gaps in Georgia’s Blood Mountain Wilderness. Hikers who didn’t want to tote a hard-sided container could simply avoid camping in many of those.

“The ATC has recommended that overnight campers on the Trail carry a bear-resistant food storage container since 2017 because of how adept bears have become at defeating traditional food hangs and other storage methods,” Somerville said. “This new order along the AT in Georgia will require all overnight hikers and backpackers to use reliable food storage gear—a hard-sided bear canister—on their AT adventures, which will protect themselves and the bears that call the AT home.”

Getting AT thru- and section-hikers to embrace the new guidelines could be a challenge. While the ATC has recommended for almost 10 years that hikers carry bear canisters, data suggests that few do. A 2025 survey by The Trek found that 13.6 percent used a canister, compared to 43 percent who used a bear hang and 32.3 percent who chose the riskiest option and slept with their food.

#8276. Are Ultralight, Ultrastrong Dyneema Rain Mitts Worth Hikers’ Money? We Tested Them.

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

In Gimmick or Gamechanger, the Backpacker editors test hiking gadgets to see what’s worth your money—and what’s a waste of it.

I’ve backpacked in my fair share of nasty conditions. On Vancouver Island’s West Coast Trail, I trudged through a downpour so heavy that I had to wring out my pants by the time I got to camp. In Gates of the Arctic National Park, I wore neoprene socks over my Darn Toughs to trap some warmth in my feet as I slogged through boggy tundra. Wet conditions, even when temperatures are mild, can be the most difficult in which to stay warm and comfortable. Looking back, I wish I had packed some rain mitts on those trips.

Most backpackers aren’t carrying waterproof overmitts. They serve a niche purpose of keeping your hands dry in wet but warm(ish) weather. In truly cold conditions, you need heavy-duty gloves. For summer showers, you can usually go without gloves or mitts entirely. But for hikes in steady rain with temperatures in the 40s and 50s? Rain mitts can work wonders to maintain comfort while taking up minimal space and weight in your pack.

As a hiker based in the PNW, I was excited when I came across a pair of ultralight rain mitts from cottage brand High Tail Designs, which is known for colorful printed fabrics and artist collaborations. Made for use alone or with a liner glove for warmth, they employ a blend of Dyneema Composite Fabric (DCF) and Dyneema Hybrid Fabric and weigh roughly an ounce per pair. They also run a whopping $105. What sets them apart from most other rain mitts on the market is the material and the fun aesthetics. Few other brands use Dyneema for hiking apparel; it shows up mostly in products like backpacks and shelters where strength is paramount. It’s also unusual to see Dyneema in colors other than black at white, as the material is difficult to dye.

Because it doesn’t absorb moisture, Dyneema dries faster than other waterproof materials like treated nylon. This also means it doesn’t stretch or bag out when exposed to lots of water. The flipside is that it doesn’t breathe—a Dyneema rain jacket would dry faster than a Gore-Tex one, but you’d likely be soaked from the inside after a few minutes of hiking. I wondered how those competing properties would work in a pair of rain mitts.

Off the bat, I was a fan of how the mitts protected my hands on rainy hikes. The fully taped seams kept moisture at bay, and I appreciated the large pull loops and cinchable shock cord wrists. They’re oversized for use with or without liners, so dexterity is limited, but that’s expected with any kind of mitts.

Other rain mitts, like those made with Gore-Tex, boast some level of breathability. These, in comparison, are basically a vapor barrier for your hands. They’re not meant to be breathable, and I found myself surprisingly unbothered by this. Hiking in a downpour with temperatures in the mid-50s, they kept my hands comfortable and dry, and I didn’t work up enough of a sweat over an hour to feel clammy inside. And since I care more about keeping my hands warm than dry, I don’t mind that these aren’t designed to breathe.

But does the fact that they’re made of Dyneema make them better than other rain mitts? What makes Dyneema appealing for outdoor gear is its remarkable strength-to-weight ratio, which can make all the difference in heavy-duty gear like backpacks and shelters. But it is invariably more expensive than other materials. In a small product like mittens, the weight savings become almost negligible, and the added tensile strength seems frivolous for the cost.

I haven’t done enough long-term testing of these mitts to speak to their durability over time, but I’m skeptical that they truly outlast similar products made from treated nylon. Generally, DCF is more tear-resistant than nylon, but it can also be more susceptible to abrasions and pinholes. While my pair hasn’t shown any signs of deterioration yet, the properties of DCF seem like overkill for a mitt where treated nylon will do.

Which brings me to the price. High Tail Designs’ rain mitts are $105 per pair. At 30 grams per pair (size small/medium), they are among the lightest rain mitts out there—but not by much. The Helium UL Rain Mitt from Outdoor Research costs half as much at $55, though it weighs twice as much at 68 grams per pair. Black Diamond’s UL Overmitts weigh a few grams less (23 grams for a size small) and are still more affordable at $70. I haven’t personally tested either of those mitts, but they are comparable in weight and function at a much lower price point.

As someone who hikes in everything from a drizzle to a deluge, I’m a rain mitt convert. I’ll be wearing these all winter long for lowland romps where fully weatherproof, insulated gloves are overkill but liners alone would soak through. They’ll also have a place in my pack on wet overnights or long-distance summer hikes where I need some just-in-case protection and don’t want to pack heavy gloves.

In my opinion, rain mitts as a category are a gamechanger. But it’s extremely hard to justify $105 for a pair made from the highest-end ultralight materials when there are cheaper options on the market that function similarly. For that reason, Dyneema rain mitts feel more like a gimmick. However, if you’re someone who puts a high value on style, that added cost may be worth it. High Tail Designs sells rain mitts in 11 different patterns; their company ethos is all about self-expression on the trail, and their colorful designs support real artists.

#8275. Shah Daulat, a Celebrated Alpinist Who Summited K2, Dies at 31

Shah Daulat, 31, was raised in the mountains of Shimshal, a remote village in Pakistan’s Hunza Valley that has encouraged and supported generations of the country’s strongest climbers. In his early years of being a professional guide with the Karakoram Mountain Guides Association, Daulat climbed four of the world’s 8,000-meter peaks, cementing his legacy as one of Pakistan’s rising alpinists.

“His journey from a mountain guide to climbing some of the world’s most challenging peaks is something our family is incredibly proud of,” Ibadat said. “He dedicated his life to the mountains and was deeply passionate about climbing.”

Daulat began working as a guide in 2022, and his progression onto the world’s highest peaks came quickly. That year, he summited K2, at 8,611 meters the second-highest mountain in the world. In 2023, he climbed 8,126-meter Nanga Parbat without supplemental oxygen, followed by Gasherbrum II in 2024. In 2025, he summited Gasherbrum I, again without supplemental oxygen, marking his fourth 8,000-meter summit in as many years. That same year, he also climbed Laila Peak, a 6,096-meter mountain in Pakistan’s Hushe Valley.

But his life in the mountains extended far beyond expedition climbing. He was a skier, too, competing at Malam Jabba in northern Pakistan in 2022. And though his career took him to some of the highest vistas in the world, it was on a much smaller objective, close to home, that he passed.

On February 6, 2026, Daulat was ice climbing near Khyber village in Gojal, Hunza, when he fell nearly 400 meters. Local volunteers recovered his body, which was later returned to his home village of Shimshal for burial.

After his death, Daulat’s cousin, pioneering Pakistani mountaineer Samina Baig, remembered both what he had accomplished in a remarkably short climbing career and the person behind those achievements. “Shah Daulat was a true gem in our family—a cherished younger brother (cousin) taken from us far too soon,” Baig wrote in a Facebook tribute. “A young mountaineer, he achieved so much in such a short life, touching many hearts with his courage and gentle spirit.

“May he rest in peace among the mountains he loved,” she continued. “He will forever remain in our hearts, remembered with love and quiet pride.”

In September, the villages of Shimsal and Khyber jointly installed a life-sized memorial sculpture of Daulat near the Khyber Ice Wall, which has been renamed the Shah Daulat Ice Wall.

#8273. Hike of the Week: Explore a Wilderness With Wolves and Endless Flat-Topped Peaks

The Flat Tops Wilderness Area in northwestern Colorado is one of my favorite places to drop off-grid. Among its basalt peaks and sweeping valleys are some of the state’s best trails, in my opinion. Its “hidden-gem” days are long gone—lots of people, especially those from Colorado’s Western Slope, recreate here. Yet, you can still find areas where you’re the only human for miles.

That solitude can be intoxicating. The 10.9-mile out-and-back to Marvine Lakes via the Marvine Trail could easily be a dayhike. But when I visited with a group of friends this summer, we wanted to spend time marinating in the scenery, lounging on the lakes’ shoreline with some beers, and enjoying a nice bagged meal with friends. I saw more wildlife on that trip than I have on any other in a long time: We crossed paths with elk, mule deer, beavers, and a silver-colored canid that looked much bigger than any coyote I’ve ever seen. Was it a wolf? I can’t say with certainty, but the Flat Tops is one of the areas where Colorado’s wolf reintroduction program has been most successful.

The trail starts at East Marvine Campground, about 35 miles east of Meeker. When we arrived, several outfitters were saddling horses and preparing to ride out with their groups. The trail is multi-use, though mountain bikes and motorized vehicles are not permitted in wilderness areas. Dogs are allowed, and leashes are not required. But hikers should stay both stay horse- and bear-aware.

The hike itself isn’t too strenuous, climbing just 1,045 feet over the 5.4 miles to the lakes. It passes small beaver ponds, pops out into meadows where you might catch a glimpse of browsing elk or deer, and winds through thick old-growth pine and spruce forest. The hike follows pristine Marvine Creek the entire way. Water is never an issue as long as you’ve got a means of purifying it.

When you arrive at lower Marvine Lake, you’ll find turquoise water reflecting the stratigraphy of the towering cliffs that hem the valley. The trail splits and goes around both sides of the lake, passing dispersed camping spots. We picked one on the very far end of lower Marvine Lake, between it and upper Marvine Lake. Our group hung out well past dark, expecting the kind of stars that only the remote corners of the Rockies can deliver. We were not disappointed.

We hiked out the next day, retracing our footsteps to the trailhead. If you wanted a longer hike, the Marvine Trail extends deeper east into the Flat Tops Wilderness Area and connects to an entire trail network. Following it all the way out to Twin Lakes and returning via the East Marvine Lakes Trail would make a 22.5-mile loop and end at the same trailhead you started at, with more alpine ponds and lakes along the way.

#8270. 10 Simple Ways to Raise Kids Who Make Good Decisions

Ask any parent what it’s like to raise a kid today, and we’d likely tell you modern childhood seems much more complex—and perilous—than when we were young. Thanks to increased peer pressure, massive technological advances, and on-demand access to virtually anything via click or tap, kids today face a wider array of choices and decision-making opportunities than we did when we were their age.

As parents, we hope we’ve instilled strong values and resilience in our children so they’re always able to make good decisions. But how can we be sure they’ll do the right thing, especially when we’re not around? While there’s no magic formula, here are 10 tips to help your kid make smart decisions—even when you’re not there.

The earlier parents initiate conversations about how to make good decisions with their kids, the better. Explaining to your child what it means to make a good decision and why it’s important can set them up for future success. Kevin Zoromski, a psychologist and early childhood development expert says, “Give children choices as part of their day and as part of their typical routine. They will look forward to having some say over what they get to do in the household and you will establish their sense of responsibility as important decision-makers.”

Kids learn through observation and patterning the behaviors of people in their lives, especially their parents. Modeling good decision-making behavior will help reinforce your life lessons. Show your kid that you are honest, responsible, and accountable for your choices. “You are your child’s first and most important role model,” said mental health expert Ketsupa Jirakarn. “[Kids] are always observing and learning from you every day—even when you are unaware of it. So, make sure you practice what you preach.”

Let your kids know what you expect from them in terms of making smart decisions. For older kids, this could include things like always telling you where they are going, not using illicit substances like drugs and alcohol, and staying away from dangerous situations. “Children are more likely to accept the limits you set and are more likely to want to meet your expectations (i.e., be responsible) when you provide a warm, caring, and supportive relationship that underlies the discipline you impose,” according to a report from The Center for Parenting Education.

Give your child opportunities to practice smart decision-making. This could involve giving them small choices, such as what to wear to school or what to eat for dinner. It also could involve giving them bigger choices, such as whether to join a sports team or what to do with their allowance. By empowering your child to learn about the consequences of their choices through smaller actions, they will feel more empowered when making bigger decisions on their own.

When your kid makes a mistake, don’t immediately swoop in to fix the problem or resort immediately to punishment. Help them understand why a misstep was a consequence of not making the best decision, and then talk about how they can make a better choice next time. According to a report from the Harvard Graduate School of Education, “Reframing mistakes as opportunities from which we can learn—rather than failures alone—can help us feel like we are capable and in control. Reframing can also help us handle future mistakes more effectively.”

Learning how to think critically and independently requires self-awareness (i.e., knowing strengths, weaknesses, and values) as well as problem-solving skills. Encouraging your child to think through a decision and come up with a solution can further nurture and develop their critical thinking skills. “In childhood and adolescence, the body goes through many physical changes, but there are also many changes in how we think, feel, and behave, and in our motivations,” according to a report from Frontiers for Young Minds. It’s through repeated trial and error that kids develop the necessary skills to thrive into adulthood.

Some decisions have few consequences, while other decisions are highly consequential. Teaching your child the difference between big and small choices, and understanding the risks associated with some decisions will mitigate the chances of bad outcomes. For example, teach young kids about the risks of eating too much junk food or overdoing it with screen time, and teach older kids about the risks of cyberbullying and underage drinking.

Talk to your child about the choices they’re facing and help them understand the different options and the potential consequences of each choice. Teaching them how to evaluate information, identify biases, and make informed decisions as well as helping your child understand and manage their emotions and how to make decisions that are in line with their values will serve them well. “Emotional literacy starts at birth when babies can just bond with [their parents] and connect on just that level. And it continues to evolve,” said Dr. Michele Borba, parenting expert and author of Building Moral Intelligence: The Seven Essential Virtues that Teach Kids to Do the Right Thing.

As parents, being supportive and consistent with our reactions to our children’s choices will help ensure they make smart ones, even when we’re not present. If you sometimes let your child get away with making a bad decision, they will be less likely to take you seriously when you expect them to make good choices without you. Additionally, when your kid makes a good decision, be sure to praise and validate them. “Youth who experience more positive interactions with parents are better adjusted. Indeed, consistency in parenting—primarily consistency in discipline—has been linked to more positive youth outcomes,” according to a report from the National Institutes of Health.

It takes time for kids to learn how to make smart decisions. Don’t get discouraged if they don’t always and immediately make the right choices. Even when your kids are old enough to make decisions themselves, they still need your patience and understanding. Be there to talk to them, offer advice, and help them deal with the consequences of their decisions.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8267. How to Make a Handprint Calendar

Hanging around the house for the holidays? Spend an afternoon or two working on a handprint calendar for 2027. It’s an easy project anyone can complete, and little helpers will love to lend a hand or two. After all, you’ve got a long winter break to fill with activities and printables, and by New Year’s Eve, you’ll have reached the point where painting your kids’ hands sounds like a rational idea!

We love this project because there’s no right way to make one. Keep it simple, or get super crafty— it’s all up to your kids’ imagination. Use the guide below to get started, and decide in advance what you’ll make out of each handprint. This is much easier to do before your little helper has paint all over their hands!

Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027

Paint your kids’ hands with the selected colors and have them make a print on each piece of paper. Colored paper is also an option if you want to use white paint (see January and October). Depending on your design, you may need just one handprint, a fingerprint, or even a footprint. Be sure to wash and dry your hands between each month, and continue through the year, from January to December. If you think it doesn’t look like much, don’t worry! After each month has dried, and you add the details, it’ll look awesome.

Insider Tip: Let your kids have some input with this project. While you may have a perfect vision in mind for how to execute a gorgeous Christmas tree using their sweet little hands, they might have another idea, and that’s okay.

Now that you have all of the months ready to go (and dry!), it’s time to put your calendar together. The easiest way to go is to order a ready-made blank calendar, such as this blank wall calendar from Amazon. For under $10, you won’t have to mess with binding or stapling, or fussing with the assembly of the calendar—glue or use double-sided tape to attach your own homemade monthly pictures to the blank template and you’re good to go.

Related: New Year’s Eve Confetti Poppers You Can Make with the Kids

Print out a blank 2023 calendar from Calendar Labs. One by one, place the pages behind the handprint so that when it flips upward, you’ll have the right picture and month. For example, the calendar days for January should be glued to the February picture, the calendar days for February should be glued to March, and so on.

Insider Tip: Make sure to place the calendar month on the backside and bottom of the handprint, so as you flip each month, the painted picture is positioned the correct way.

Once you’ve glued all the calendar pages to the handprints, use the laminating sleeves to seal each one. Follow the instructions on the package, and use a ruler to eliminate any air pockets or creases.

Using a hole punch, make three holes at the top of each page (the calendar month should have the holes at the top) and one hole at the bottom (this is where the calendar will hang on the wall).

Then, using string or thin twine, run a length through each of the three holes and tie it up like you would a book (it should open from the right side). That’s it! You’ll have a fun keepsake that will hang around for an entire year.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8265. Sleep-Unders Are Honestly a Win for Everyone

As soon as kids hit school age, the pressure of the sleepover begins. Whether your little one wants to host a crew of first graders in your living room (hard pass) or is being asked to sleep over at someone else’s house, there are a lot of questions that come with the milestone. Will my kid have fun? Will they sleep at all? Will they be overwhelmed? Add to that concerns surrounding safety, and it’s a tough position for parents to be in. The solution: the “sleep-under.”

The sleep-under brings the best elements of the sleepover and avoids the actual sleeping-over part. It’s become a trendy birthday party theme because it puts less pressure on kids and the parents hosting. How it works is that kids show up to the host house all ready for a sleepover, usually around dinner time. Guests might even arrive decked out in their coziest PJs to add to the whole sleepover vibe. The group enjoys pizza, watches a movie, plays some games, and does an activity like decorating cupcakes.

All the festivities are concluded just before bedtime, when parents return to swoop up their little ones and everyone heads back home to sleep in their own beds. Nobody is over-tired the next day. Nobody needs to call home for a late-night pickup when they have a nightmare. No parent has to stress over whether it’s a good idea to leave their kid overnight with someone they only know from the pick-up line. No kid has to feel ashamed if they aren’t yet ready to sleep away from their parents for the night. The sleep-under side-steps all those potential issues.

Honestly, it’s pretty genius. We just wish it were a thing when we were kids!

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8262. 21 Easy Play Ideas for Kids (Whether You Have 5, 15, or 30 Minutes)

Between daily parenting duties, work, and navigating the current world in general, saying your days are full is probably an understatement. And while your kid’s day may be full of exploration and creativity, they can also experience a lot of anxiety, stress, and pressure. That makes it even more important to have some positive, uninterrupted time to reconnect.

Even five minutes can make a difference in a child’s emotional well-being. But as Randy McCoy, VP of Product & Curriculum for The Little Gym, reminds us, how long you play is less important than how often. “It’s not necessarily the ‘duration of play’ but the ‘frequency of play’ that matters most,” Mccoy says. “If a parent can give their child their undivided attention and play with them just five minutes a day, every day, they’re on the right track.”

The good news is, there are lots of ways to play that take next-to-no prep. Read on for 21 easy ideas to play with your kids, whether you have five minutes, 15, or more.

When you have a few minutes, whether it’s before school or after dinner, bust out these little-to-no-prep basics you can use just about anywhere.

1. Try out “Would You Rather?” kid edition. Spend a fun five minutes taking turns asking questions like, “Would you rather never eat ice cream again or get a trampoline?” or “Ride a dinosaur for 20 miles or an elephant for an hour?” The sillier the better. This also makes a great road trip game.

2. Make a dictionary dash. Grab a dictionary and choose a word at random. Read it out loud and have the kids guess what it means. If they can read, they can take turns finding words and trying to stump you.

3. Tickle your sidekick’s funny bone. Whip out brain busters or riddles that will make them laugh. Luckily, you don’t need Comedy Central writers for this one. We think your goofballs will get a kick out of our ultimate list of jokes for kids.

4. A few rounds of “We’re going on a picnic” alphabet-style will entertain the tot lot. The first player up says, “I’m going on a picnic,” then adds a tasty packable to the phrase, like an apple, apricot, or avocado. Stick with ABC order or focus on just one letter for each round.

5. Play 20 questions. Have your kids guess what you’re thinking of, and keep it simple, like something you can see from where you’re standing.

6. Play a classic game of Rock, Paper, Scissors—Japanese style. It’s called Janken. Start by saying “saisho wa guu.” Then “janken pon” as you pump, before throwing on “pon.” The winning combos are still the same in this timeless, quick game you can play at home or on the go.

7. Turn yourself into a living “spot the difference” puzzle. Start with a slow model turn, then disappear and make a quick change out of sight. When you come back, your cutie’s got to spot what’s different. Did you take off a cap? Put on a scarf? Untie a shoe? Keep it easy for the tots, and kick it up a notch for older kiddos (only one earring!). Then let them have a turn trying to stump you.

8. Try out a sequencing game when the wanderlust takes hold. Name a person, place, and object, all starting with the same letter of the alphabet, then string them together like kids lining up for the school bus. “Alice from Australia loves alligators!” See how far you can get in a short amount of time.

For parents, playing with our kids allows us to step out of all those daily parental duties and, as McCoy explains, build friendship between parent and child. “It provides an opportunity for you to interact with them on a different level,” he says. “For a special moment, you step out of the ‘parent’ role and step into a playmate role.”  Take a break from your to-do list and try one of these 15-minute ideas that will thrill the kids and relax you, too.

9. Post-It style. A stack of Post-It notes and a pen are all it takes to play this short-and-sweet variation of the classic guessing game for parties. Choose someone to be “it.” Write on the Post-It note the name of a character from a book, movie, or show that your kid will recognize—it can be a famous person, someone they know, or a fictional character. Stick the note to their forehead, without letting them see what you wrote. Now take turns going around the room giving “it” clues to help them guess who is on their head.

10. Curl up with a good book. Putting out a basket of books in a central location motivates the kids to take a look through the pages when they’ve got time to spare. Add in a sweet bookmark that keeps track of time to make it count.

11. Give them their daily feels. Keep your favorite sensory bin fillers on hand (like cotton balls and dry beans), along with trinkets to bury and cups for spilling and filling. When you’ve got a short window, pull out the bin, fill ‘er up, and watch your kids dig and drizzle until it’s time to go.

12. Set up a quick cotton ball and straw race. Perfect for the kitchen table before lunch is served. Have siblings challenge each other for the pole position on a straightaway down the center of the table, or set up a simple obstacle course using cups that the kiddos have to work around. Ready, set, go!

13. Give a penny for their thoughts when they write in a journal. Setting aside a short amount of time to write (each day!) is a great way to encourage your amateur author’s creativity. Use silly or thought-provoking prompts to get them thinking, like, “The first time I tried …” or “When I get to be principal, I’ll …” or even “The craziest thing that happened today…” Write on, brother!

14. Give up the charade. Have your little monkey stay in character when you play a quick game of animal charades. No prep is necessary for this easy guessing game. Just pick your favorite animal and go for it! With each successful guess, trade places and start again. Ee-i-ee-i-o!

Whether your aim is active playtime or quiet(er) crafting time, filling a cool 30 minutes with your kids is easier than you think. It may take a bit of planning, but once the prep is done, it’s a sit-back-and-relax situation that’s well worth the time upfront.

15. All things LEGO. If LEGO was the first thing that popped into your head, then we’re right there with you. They’re the forever fallback for a reason, but to hit that half-hour sweet spot, try throwing a LEGO challenge into the mix: building a car that can also work underwater, or constructing a tower that’s at least 24 inches tall. Then let your master-builder go to work.

16. Spin them right round. Ana at Babble Dabble Do has a new way to play with Perler beads. She puts them to work teaching science and playing tricks when these melted beauties become spinning tops. It’s just the right amount of make-and-play to fill a brief window in your busy day.

17. One for the movers and shakers. Print out (and laminate if you’re feeling bold) The Alerting Activity Game, designed by Training Happy Hearts. Keep the deck on hand to stack the odds in your favor when the kids need something to do. With simple activities like “jump up and down ten times” or “pretend to be a volcano,” it’s packed with energy-burning activities that kids can run through on their own or with you!

18. Bring the outside in and paint it. If snow isn’t covering your yard, go for a hunt for leaves, evergreen boughs, and sticks. Then take your findings to the craft table to fancy them up with paint. Acrylics work great for this project.

For activities that span the hour, the two-step Make & Play approach works well. You may want to do a little prep the day before to make it easier, like putting crafting necessities into one small bin that you can pull out to surprise the kids.

19. Wage war. Ah, the classic card game that is so simple to learn and so hard to win. It is possible that a game of war can take longer than one hour, but it rarely takes less. You do two card battles with the highest card the winner until one person has all the cards. Get the complete rules here.

20. Create a mini catapult. Little Bins for Little Hands has an awesome tutorial, using craft sticks and other office supplies you’re sure to have around the house. Once it’s built, set up target practice plates before letting the marshmallows fly.

21. Put on a show. Puppets never get old; they’re easy to make with an old sock, brown paper lunch bag, or even familiar characters glued to craft sticks. Whatever method you choose, spend time creating and playing with puppets when you’ve got an hour or more to spare. Be sure to stock the craft bin with all kinds of googly eyes, buttons, yarn, and doo-dads to help bring your buddies to life. Then find an old sheet or use a baby’s blanket draped over the table to create a stage. Bravo!

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8258. 41 Elf on the Shelf Ideas (Because You’re Gonna Need Them)

It’s that time again. Yup, your Elf on the Shelf is about to parachute in to make your life (slightly) more challenging for the next few weeks. Get ahead of the game and prep your bag of tricks with these brilliant ideas. From Elf on the Shelf clothes to last-minute Elf on the Shelf ideas that’ll make the whole family giggle, we’ve got enough easy Elf ideas to last you the entire holiday season.

I remember when my kids were little, and they got their first elves. Not going to lie, remembering to move the thing every night was a struggle. But when I made the effort and managed to pull off even the easiest of Elf ideas, the look in their eyes was priceless.

1. Elf held captive. If you have two Scout elves, this easy Elf idea is a lot of fun. Pull out a toy train and a string, and decide which elf is going to be extra naughty by tying up the other one.

2. Plan a hot cocoa party. This is fun on the first night or maybe on a weekend day. Get mugs, instant cocoa, and marshmallows set up in advance and settle the elves against the mugs. Snag printables for the party here.

3. Spell it out. Do you have Scrabble tiles or Bananagrams? Then it’s a cinch to let your elf leave a sweet message for your littles to discover the next day.

4. Caught in the act. With this easy elf idea, you’ll use a bag of M&Ms, chocolate chips, or even a box of sugar cereal, and position your elf with its backside out of the bag.

5. Exhausted elf. All those trips up to the North Pole make for one tired elf. Let your little one in red take a day off. Make them a little bed with a doll blanket and a cotton ball for a pillow.

6. Deeds worth doing. Since reporting good deeds to Santa is your elf’s duty, it’s the perfect opportunity to remind kids about the spirit of Christmas. We dig the free downloadable from Over the Big Moon.

7. Elf spaghetti. Whip up Buddy the Elf’s favorite dish for your little helper. Hint: this is a great idea for the night you make pasta. You’ll also need syrup (of course), marshmallows, candy, and chocolate syrup. Find out how to make a batch over at Instructables.

8. Riding the banister. Those naughty elves are always looking for an adrenaline rush! Use a Frisbee and sticky tape to get your little buddy set up at the top and ready to ride.

9. Sitting pretty. Have your elf take a seat inside your wreath or on the holiday table for a picture-perfect spot.

10. Play games. Set up your elf mid-move with this adorable mini-Twister printable.

11. Window view. If you’ve got a window and a curtain rod, you’ve got a sweet spot to hang your elf. Easy-peasy.

12. Rock climbing wall. All you need is several pre-made bows to make a route for your elf.

13. Coloring elf. Take 30 seconds to scribble in a coloring book or on a printable, scatter crayons, and set up your elf. Giggles are guaranteed!

15. Zipline. This Elf on the Shelf idea is popular, but it does take a little time to set up. All you need is string or yarn, a candy cane, and a way to secure your elf to the candy cane!

16. LEGO throne. Whether you use DUPLO or LEGO, making a seat for Santa’s little helper can be done in less than five minutes.

17. Elf in the kitchen. Got a play kitchen? Then let your elf whip up something yummy.

18. On the road. With a toy car, your elf can go just about anywhere they want to go. Headed to buy a Christmas tree? Done. Want to take Wonder Woman out on a date? Totally!

19. Play Picasso. A dry-erase marker, a family photo, and a sense of humor are all you need. Give your kids beards and cat ears: See how much they laugh!

20. Put the elf in the freezer. Your elf sure does miss the North Pole! Give him a little time to chill.

21. Toilet paper tricks. Add an elf to a roll of toilet paper and send them down the stairs. Don’t have a second level? Leave a trail of written messages down the hall instead.

22. Bath time. You don’t need a Barbie bath to let your Elf soak aching bones— a plastic bowl or storage container will do the trick. Add marshmallows for bubbles, and you’re set.

23. Gone fishing. Your kids will love waking up to find the elf “fishing” for goldfish crackers in the bathroom sink.

24. Story time. Position the elf with a favorite holiday book and a captivated audience.

25. Hanging by a limb. Any elf will feel right at home when dangling from a branch of the Christmas tree.

26. Spa day. Wrap your elf in a paper towel, give them cucumber eye patches, and just like that, it’s a spa day.

27. Puzzle play. Settling your elf in for the night with a puzzle is easy and fun.

28. Paper bag race. Take those lunch bags that have been cluttering your drawer and collect a few stuffies. Then, stage a sack race-style scene across your dining room table or kitchen island.

29. Elfie selfie. Position your elf in front of the family laptop and snap a picture. Just be forewarned, if it’s a laptop you use, you’ll need to get it set back up before the kids get home from school.

30. Sweet snow angels. It’s not quite as cold down here as it is at the North Pole. When your elf gets antsy for chilly weather, make them a personal snow angel. You can use flour (but it’s messy), sprinkles, or rice, which is my personal favorite because it’s the easiest to clean up!

31. All wrapped up. Give your elf the scissors, tape, and wrapping paper. Scatter shredded paper and tape around, and it’ll be like they were caught in the act of wrapping up Santa’s gifts!

32. Elf making popcorn. Someone’s ready for family movie night!

33. Don’t move the elf. Well, it looks like your kids were so well-behaved that no North Pole reporting was needed. It’s also the perfect excuse for one of those nights you forget to move them.

34. Cards, anyone? Didn’t you know elves love to play games? They do, and they love to be caught mid-game.

35. A Stuck Elf. This is a super-easy elf idea, and you don’t even need the message board to pull it off. Just grab a mason jar or an empty water bottle and a prominent place to display your elf’s tight situation.

36. S’more to love. Some toothpicks, roasted marshmallows, chocolate squares, graham crackers, and tea lights are all you need to set up this cozy and easy elf idea.

37. Read all about it. Prop them up on a favorite Christmas story or beloved book.

38. Caught red-handed. Have your elf stage a scene of questionable actions and tape up the area with crepe paper.

39. Photo editor. They can’t help but make mischief, and marking up a festive photo is a silly way to say, “Elf wuz here.”

40. Riding dinos. If you’ve got a plastic dinosaur (T. rex preferred), then you’ve got what you need to give your elf a prehistoric ride.

41. Send the Elf back to the North Pole. Possibly one of our favorite easy elf ideas: on Christmas Morning, make sure they’re out of sight, and of course, leave a note.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8256. Don’t Throw Away Your Pumpkin Yet! Try These 6 Easy Ways to Use It in Your Yard After Halloween

Most carved pumpkins tend to get binned or left rotting on the curb once the candles burn out. Yet that leftover gourdish grin is packed with benefits for your soil, future plants, and wildlife

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The first few days of November bring a familiar sorry sight, as pumpkins start piling up beside the trash cans, a few of them still grinning. Millions end up in landfills every year, where they break down without much air and give off greenhouse gases. That's a poor end for leftover Halloween pumpkins. In a garden, all that soft tissue could be breaking down into organic matter and feeding soil life – and that’s just the start.

If you took the time to grow pumpkins for Halloween, you know how much space, moisture, and fertilizer a single vine demands. All summer long, its leaves absorbed sunlight and pumped nutrients directly into its swollen fruit. Letting those nutrients leave your yard in a trash bag deprives your yard of valuable goodness that could be benefiting vegetable beds, feeding organisms and helping beneficial creatures. Even a carved pumpkin can have a second life as long as it hasn't been painted or coated.

Giving your post-Halloween gourds a productive second act is simple, fun, and satisfying. The only rule is that your fruit needs to be clean and free of contaminants. Any sections coated in craft paints, glitter, chemical sealants, or fake snow must be removed and tossed into the trash. Pull out any burnt candle stubs, melted wax, and battery-powered tea lights, and you are ready to put this fall bounty to work!

Turning post-holiday pumpkins into garden assets is a real no-brainer. Standard carving pumpkin varieties like Howden and Jack O' Lantern work especially well for the soil, because their flesh is tender and relatively easy to slice. Thicker, denser culinary and heirloom varieties (such as ribbed Cinderella, dusty-blue Jarrahdale, or warty Marina di Chioggia) offer firmer rinds that hold their shape for weeks, making them ideal where shape and rigidity are useful.

These fall projects work across every USDA hardiness zone, though local temperatures will determine how quickly your gourd decomposes. In cold northern regions (zones 3-5), freezing nights preserve carved pumpkins on porches longer, but freeze-thaw cycles eventually cause cell walls to collapse into watery slop, making early November the best time to act. In warm southern places (zones 8-10), elevated daytime temperatures accelerate mold and fruit flies, requiring immediate conversion into ground-based or wildlife-specific benefits.

Before tackling these projects, you need the right hand tools. A heavy-duty hori-hori knife is an excellent investment if you don’t have one, and can be used to simplify all kinds of cutting work. The Nisaku Hori-Hori from Amazon is great value and makes slicing through thick rinds a joy, and levers drainage holes through thick base walls without snapping. So find out exactly why your grinning pumpkin still has lots of goodness to give…

Tossing an intact pumpkin onto your compost heap can lead to disappointment. Its waxy rind acts like a raincoat, and depending on the variety and the weather, it could sit there for a long time with its skin intact. It needs breaking up first. Take a sharp spade or round-point shovel, and break the fruit down into fist-sized chunks to expose the flesh to soil bacteria and fungi.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Because the tissue is roughly 90% water, this green compost source needs plenty of dry browns mixed in. Balance every bucket of chopped pumpkin with two buckets of carbon-rich browns, such as shredded leaves, straw, or torn cardboard to keep the pile aerated. Turn the heap now and then. If space is tight, a single-chamber tumbler like the Vivosun Outdoor Dual Chamber Tumbling Composter, available from Amazon speeds up heat decomposition in a more compact way.

If your compost heap is overflowing, try direct trench composting in an empty veg bed. Dig a trench 18-24 inches (45-61cm) deep, in a bed reserved for heavy-feeding spring crops like sweet corn, squash, or tomatoes. Fill the bottom with chopped chunks and stomp them down. Backfill with 12 inches (30cm) of clean soil. Don’t go shallower, or neighborhood raccoons may smell it and dig it back up. Loose, well-drained soil can break it down in 2-3 months, but if you have heavy clay soil, you may still hit chunks of pumpkin a year from now, so be patient.

A healthy, mature Halloween pumpkin contains hundreds of plump seeds loaded with goodness. If your pumpkin grew with vibrant color and a firm rind, these seeds are prime candidates for saving for next year. Strain the tangled seed mass in a colander and massage it under a stream of cold running tap water to strip away the pulp. Spread the cleaned seeds in a single layer over non-stick parchment paper, a fine metal screen, or a ceramic plate. Let them dry in a warm, well-ventilated room out of direct sunlight for 2-3 weeks.

To test for dryness, try bending one: if it flexes, it still retains moisture, but if it snaps in half, your seeds are ready to store. Slide your dried seeds into breathable kraft paper seed envelopes. Pour them into paper seed envelopes, like the Seed Packet Kraft Envelopes, available from Walmart in packs of 100. Write the variety and date on the front, and store in a cool, dark drawer. Word to the wise, though: modern carving pumpkins are typically hybrids that won’t go true to type. Also, bees can cross-pollinate squash varieties across neighborhood zucchinis, so next spring’s seedlings may produce some wacky, unpredictable gourds.

Songbirds burn through vital fat stores as November temperatures drop, and a firm pumpkin makes a wonderful natural feeding bowl (although it’s best to stick to uncarved porch pumpkins for this project). Cut your pumpkin in half across the middle, or slice the top third off. Using a sturdy spoon or hori-hori to scrape out the inner pulp and seeds, until the interior walls are clean. Poke 3-4 half-inch (1.25cm) drainage holes through the base using a large screwdriver.

Punch 3 evenly spaced holes along the thick top rim, thread some sturdy jute twine through, and hang the bowl from a sturdy tree limb or pergola beam. Alternatively, set the flat shell on a low wall, tree stump, or deck railing. Fill with black-oil sunflower seeds or a good seed blend, such as Pennington Wild Bird Food from The Home Depot. You can also use some of your rinsed and dried pumpkin seeds as extra treats. These nutritious kitchen scraps make a nourishing treat for cardinals, blue jays and titmice. Just inspect every few days: when the inner walls turn squishy or develop fuzz, take the feeder down and consign it to the compost heap.

If you have a solid (again, uncarved) ornamental pumpkin on your porch, you can turn it into a temporary planter. Carve a generous opening around the stem and scoop out the pulp and seeds. Using a long screwdriver, puncture 4-5 generous drainage holes through the bottom crust. If you need a good screwdriver, Black Canyon’s Phillips Extended Length Screwdriver with Soft Grip Ergonomic Handle from Walmart is an efficient way to punch through thick rinds. Elevate the pumpkin on some stone or a trivet for drainage, as sitting water will rot the base rapidly.

Fill the lower half of the pumpkin with light, free-draining potting soil, then tuck in your choice of cold-tolerant fall ornamentals. Some great options include dwarf flowering kales, ruffled ornamental cabbages, winter violas, pansies, and trailing English ivy. These cold-hardy choices will look fresh and colorful for 2-4 weeks. With wet soil sitting inside it, the pumpkin starts softening from the inside out, and a few freeze-thaw nights will hurry it along. When yours starts to sag, move the plants to a bed or regular pot, and compost the gourd.

Slugs and garden snails are a persistent menace in fall, but at night they seek shelter in dark, damp, sheltered crevices to conserve moisture. A curved chunk of pumpkin rind provides a perfect natural decoy. Take sections of rind, including leftover pieces from carving or scraps that have softened too much for bird feeders. Place them skin-side up on the soil, beside vulnerable vegetable rows, hosta crowns, or mulched borders. The sweet scent of decaying squash flesh will attract slugs from several feet away, luring them under the hollowed domes.

Early the following morning, flip the rinds over. You should find dozens of slugs, snails, and earwigs clinging to the flesh. Scrape them off into a bucket of warm soapy water, or feed them to backyard chickens. Reset the traps for several nights in a row. Every slug removed now is one fewer laying eggs. Once the rind collapses, compost it. Dust a little Harris Food Grade Diatomaceous Earth Powder, available from Amazon, around your traps to stop slugs escaping back into your beds.

This last one is a lovely eco-friendly bonus for anyone keen to support overwintering beneficial insects in their yard. As fall frosts intensify, beneficial predatory insects and pollinators seek sheltered crevices. Ground beetles, centipedes, roving rove beetles, lacewings, lady bugs, and solitary native bees are valuable allies in the organic garden, consuming thousands of aphids, slug eggs, and weed seeds. You can turn a hollowed pumpkin shell into a cozy winter sanctuary. Take an uncarved or cleanly carved pumpkin. Slice a wide entryway near the base (or prop the shell upside-down on a couple of flat stones to leave an open gap underneath).

Stuff the cavity with natural textural materials that create micro-tunnels and air pockets. Use bundles of dry hollow plant stems, bamboo canes, small pine cones, crumpled dry leaves, and coarse straw. You can buy Bell Nursery Mini Straw Bales from The Home Depot which can also be used as mulch for strawberries and other overwintering plants. Tuck your bug hotel beneath a thick hedge, under a quiet shrub border, or along a perennial bed out of wind and rain. The shell will slowly soften, insulating the center. By spring, it will return harmlessly to the soil, leaving your beneficial guardians safely in the mulch bed, ready to go to work.

Before you drag your hollowed Halloween pumpkins down to the street corner, hopefully these ideas show you that they could be working hard for your yard. These seasonal gourds are far more than short-lived porch decorations. By turning into a rich soil ingredient, feeding wild birds, constructing cozy shelters for beneficial beetles and stocking up on seeds to plant next year’s pumpkins, you keep valuable resources out of landfills and grab a head start on next year's growth. Once winter sets in, those leftover gourds may already be enriching your soil: a true win-win!

A handy helper you can put out on the kitchen counter or table to keep your favorite dishes warm and ready to serve, the Lnniw White Electric Food Warming Mat is a large roll-out heating surface with different temperature levels and a timing function with six preset timer modes.

The best part of the big holiday feasts is usually the gravy for so many people, and the Nucookery Large Porcelain Gravy Boat With A Warmer can help keep your guests happy and eating throughout the entire meal. It also comes with a warming stand that you put a small votive candle in to keep the gravy warm and delicious.

#8254. The Best Nonprofits That Support Dads and Fatherhood

The best nonprofits that support dads and fatherhood.

Research has shown that when dads are engaged and present, kids do better. We celebrate dads on Father’s Day because we should celebrate everything that makes children’s lives — and outcomes — better. When children have close relationships with father figures, they tend to avoid high-risk behaviors; have higher-paying jobs and healthy, stable relationships; and have higher IQ test scores. The benefits go on, but one thing’s for sure: Dads matter in the lives of children, and so we should support and celebrate their presence in their kids’ lives.

Here are just a few organizations that champion dads and understand the integral role that fathers play in the lives of their children.

All Pro Dad is a program of Family First that provides tools and resources to dads that allow them to be more present in the lives of their children. Spearheaded by former NFL coach Tony Dungy, NFL player Benjamin Watson, ESPN personality Dan Orlovsky, and many other prominent sports figures, All Pro Dad hosts a yearly interactive get-together for kids and dads at an NFL or NCAA stadium and a monthly school program where dads meet up with their children at school to spend time bonding and relationship building.

The Center for Family Policy and Practice is a nonprofit organization that advocates for fair and equitable laws and policies that affect low-income families and fathers. Focusing on child support, family safety and security, and financial and economic security, the CFPP acts as a think tank to develop solutions to barriers experienced by low-income fathers and fathers of color.

The Child & Family Blog provides research-driven content on the impact of family on social, emotional, and cognitive child development. In addition to covering topics like race, divorce, and inequality, the Child & Family Blog covers research on the importance of fathers and the role they play in both the family dynamic and the development of children.

The Family Equality Council works to ensure that members of the LGBTQ community have the ability to create families and provide support, education, activism and advocacy, and the resources they need to become parents and foster loving, healthy family relationships. The FEP also tracks national and state legislation that affects the ability of LGBTQ couples to become parents and maintain parental rights.

Fathering Together provides anyone who identifies as a father with tools and resources to uplift and support them as they work to create a “more equitable society.” The organization hosts different communities so that dads from every walk of life can reach out to peers for help, support, and advice while working to make the world a better and safer place for their children.

The Fatherhood Project is a Massachusetts-based program that empowers fathers to become more “knowledgeable, active, and emotionally engaged with their children.” Through research-based principles and curricula and programs like Dads Matter, Dads in Recovery, Teen Dads, and Divorcing Dads, the organization aims to help all dads be more present and engaged with their children while focusing on dads in marginalized and underserved communities.

Fathers Incorporated is an Atlanta-based nonprofit that works with federal lawmakers and leaders in the responsible fatherhood movement, faith and business leaders, and family law practitioners to advocate for legislative and community changes that promote fathers’ involvement in the lives of their children. The group focuses on co-parenting, domestic violence, incarceration, child development, child support, and employment and financial stability. Fathers Incorporated provides resources and programs for fathers to engage with their children healthily and raise awareness through programs like the Million Fathers March and Black Dads Count.

Fathers’ Uplift is a one-of-a-kind organization that provides fathers with the tools they need to overcome trauma, addiction, racial barriers, and emotional issues to help them fully engage with their children and families. Fathers’ Uplift provides therapy, coaching, training opportunities, and youth enrichment with the aim of reducing the number of children raised without positive father figures in their lives. It is the only organization in the United States that offers therapy, counseling, and addiction support specifically geared toward fathers and their families with the aim of reuniting families and providing them with the framework to thrive.

The National Fatherhood Initiative is the country’s largest provider of research on the involvement of fathers and the impact fathers have on families. It provides communities with resources and training to increase father engagement with the goal of ensuring that communities and human service organizations have the tools and training they need to be father-inclusive so fathers can be more involved in the lives of their children.

The Native American Fatherhood and Families Association is an Arizona-based nonprofit focusing on nourishing family relationships through its Fatherhood Is Sacred/Motherhood Is Sacred (FIS/MIS), Linking Generations by Strengthening Relationships, and Addressing Family Violence & Abuse programs. Employing culturally sensitive curricula and materials, NAFFA is able to address the specific concerns of the Native American community to reunite families and empower fathers to become family leaders.

The National Partnership for Women and Families understands that families benefit when dads are present and actively engaged. One way the NPWF is creating a more equitable world for women is by spearheading programs, legislation, and calls to action that support fathers by promoting active fatherhood and gender equality.

Established in Brazil in 1997, Promundo has worked globally to engage fathers in the care economy, promote active fatherhood and promote gender equity and justice by engaging men and boys with women and girls. The organization is currently undergoing a rebranding to be more inclusive of all genders. Its new name, Equimundo: Center for Masculinities and Social Justice, “reflects our commitment to fostering gender equity and our roots in social justice. The name change also captures our approach of collaborating with and never overshadowing our diverse partners worldwide.”

This article was originally published on June 7, 2022
